title: Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC submits draft Resource Report Nos. 2, 3, and 8, re the Desert Southwest Expansion Project under PF26-9.

documents.text:
September 28, 2026

Ms. Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary 
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street, N.E.
Washington, D.C. 20426

Re:	Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC
	FERC Docket No. PF26-9-000
	Desert Southwest Expansion Project
	Draft Environmental Resource Reports 2, 3, and 8

Dear Ms. Reese:

On March 27, 2026, in compliance with the requirements of 18 Code of Federal Regulations ("C.F.R.") §157.21(b), Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC ("Transwestern") requested that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission ("FERC" or "Commission") begin its review of the proposed Desert Southwest Expansion Project ("Project") using FERC's Pre-Filing Review Process ("Pre-Filing"), and FERC assigned Docket No. PF26-9-000 to the Project. On April 3, 2026, FERC approved Transwestern's request.

Consistent with Section 157.21(f)(10) of the Commission's pre-filing procedures, Transwestern is filing draft Environmental Resource Reports 2, 3 and 8 for the Project. Transwestern will include final Resource Reports 2, 3 and 8 as part of the final Environmental Report as Exhibit F-1 to the certificate application, which is anticipated to be filed by November 30, 2026. 

Transwestern respectfully requests that the information submitted as Public be placed on the internet as “Public Information. 

This filing is being submitted electronically to the Commission’s eFiling website pursuant to the Commission’s Order No. 703, Filing via the Internet Guidelines, issued on November 15, 2007, in FERC Docket No. RM07-16-000. Any questions or comments regarding this filing should be directed to the undersigned at (713) 989-2605.

Respectfully submitted,


    /s/ Blair Lichtenwalter
__________________________
Blair Lichtenwalter, Sr. Director
Certificates

                               2. WATER USE AND QUALITY

2.1      INTRODUCTION

Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC (Transwestern), a wholly-owned subsidiary of Energy Transfer LP
(Energy Transfer), is seeking authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or
Commission) pursuant to Section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act to construct, own, and operate the proposed
Desert Southwest Expansion Project (Project). The Project is an expansion of the existing Transwestern
system that will consist of approximately 525.2 miles of 48-inch diameter mainline pipeline (mainline) and
approximately 180.0 miles associated with 13 lateral pipelines (laterals), as well as new compressor stations
(CS), associated meter and regulator (M&R) stations, and other aboveground facilities located in Texas,
New Mexico, and Arizona.

This Resource Report describes existing groundwater resources, surface waterbodies, water supplies,
watersheds, and wetlands potentially affected by the Project. It provides information to determine the
potential impact of the Project on water quality and use and on the measures that will be used to mitigate
the impacts. Wetland and waterbody information in this resource report summarizes the results of field
surveys conducted between December 2025 and June 2026. Wetlands and waterbodies directly affected by
or adjacent to Project facilities are shown on the alignment sheets (see Appendix 1B-1 and Appendix 1B-2
to Resource Report 1).

2.2      GROUNDWATER RESOURCES

This section describes the geology, hydrology, quality, and use of the principal aquifers within or near the
Project; the potential for impacts during construction on those aquifers; and proposed measures to mitigate
those impacts.

2.2.1 Regional Aquifers
Regional hydrogeologic conditions along the mainline and laterals were characterized using available
regional aquifer reports, including those published by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), Texas Water
Development Board (TWDB), the New Mexico Office of the State Engineer (NMOSE), and Arizona
Department of Water Resources (ADWR). The mainline and laterals traverse three principal hydrogeologic
regimes based on the USGS United States Principal Aquifer map (USGS 2003):

      1. Pecos Valley Aquifer and associated Delaware Basin bedrock aquifers in west Texas;

      2. Rio-Grande Aquifer System of western Texas and New Mexico; and

      3. Basin and Range basin-fill aquifers in Arizona.

Groundwater occurrence, depth, aquifer hydraulic properties (hydraulic conductivity and transmissivity),
confinement, and water quality vary substantially along the route as a function of basin-fill thickness,
topography, structural position, groundwater withdrawals, fine-grained confining intervals, and dissolution-
enhanced permeability within Permian carbonate and evaporite units. Characteristics for the regional
aquifers for the mainline and laterals are described in the following sections, from east to west.

2.2.1.1 Pecos Valley Aquifer and Associated Delaware Basin Bedrock Aquifers
The mainline (mileposts [MPs] 0 to 170) and the ET Orla East, RBX & Bear, and RBO laterals are underlain
by the Delaware Basin and Pecos Valley hydrogeologic setting of west Texas. Principal aquifers within this



DESERT SOUTHWEST EXPANSION PROJECT                   1                    TRANSWESTERN PIPELINE COMPANY, LLC
 RESOURCE REPORT 2                                    DRAFT                            WATER USE AND QUALITY



segment, from east to west, include the Pecos Valley Aquifer (major aquifer), Rustler Aquifer, Capitan
Reef Complex, and Bone Spring–Victorio Peak (minor aquifers) (George et al. 2011). These aquifers
include fractured Permian carbonate and evaporite units associated with the Delaware Basin, as well as
younger unconsolidated alluvial deposits associated with the Pecos Valley.

Pecos Valley Aquifer. The Pecos Valley Aquifer overlies most of the Rustler Aquifer (which also outcrops
to the west) and consists primarily of Quaternary alluvium, terrace deposits, eolian sand, and locally older
basin-fill sediments occupying the Pecos Trough and Monument Draw Trough (Ryder 1996). The Pecos
Valley Aquifer is the major aquifer along the Project in West Texas. Saturated alluvial and eolian deposits
within the Pecos Valley Aquifer are generally between 100 and 300 feet thick, but basin-fill deposits locally
exceed 1,500 feet within the Pecos Trough and Monument Draw Trough. Along the Project, the aquifer is
generally less than 600 feet thick. Groundwater is generally unconfined but may be locally confined by clay
deposits (Ryder 1996). The depth to groundwater ranges from near ground surface by the Pecos River and
irrigated areas, to local artesian conditions beneath confining beds (Ashworth et al. 1995), to more than 100
feet below ground surface (bgs) beneath uplands and developed pumping areas. Transmissivity is highly
variable depending on grain size and aquifer heterogeneity. Hydraulic conductivity value estimates near
the Project are approximately 10 to 15 feet per day (ft/d) (George et al. 2011), and well yields vary between
200 and 2,500 gallons per minute (gpm) and average about 1,000 gpm (Ryder 1996). Groundwater quality
in the Pecos Valley Aquifer is generally fresher than adjacent Delaware Basin bedrock aquifers, with many
areas containing total dissolved solids (TDS) concentrations below 1,000 milligrams per liter (mg/L);
however, elevated chloride and sulfate concentrations are common and locally exceed U.S. Environmental
Protection Agency (EPA) secondary maximum contaminant level (MCL - aesthetic standards that affect
taste, color, odor, or appearance) drinking water standards. More than 80 percent of the groundwater
pumped from the Pecos Valley Aquifer is used for irrigation, and the remaining is used for municipal,
industrial, and power generation uses (George et al. 2011).

Groundwater within the Pecos Valley Aquifer occurs primarily in unconsolidated alluvial deposits, where
aquifer yield is principally controlled by grain size and saturated thickness. Groundwater occurrence within
the Delaware Basin bedrock aquifers (described below) is controlled largely by secondary permeability
associated with fractures, joints, and solution openings in carbonate and evaporite rocks. Accordingly, well
yields may vary over relatively short distances (Ryder 1996, George et al. 2011).

Rustler Aquifer. The Rustler Aquifer consists primarily of fractured dolomite, gypsum, and anhydrite
(Ryder 1996). The Rustler Aquifer is generally 250 to more than 600 feet thick in the area it outcrops west
of the Pecos Valley Aquifer; it dips toward the center of the Delaware Basin and underlies the Pecos Valley
Aquifer. Aquifer transmissivity is generally low except where enhanced by carbonate or evaporite
dissolution. Reported well yields vary significantly and range from less than 10 gmp to more than 1,000
gpm locally (Mace et al. 2001). Reported depths to groundwater within the Rustler outcrop are generally
between 50 and 150 feet bgs. Groundwater within the aquifer is generally brackish and characterized by
elevated TDS concentrations and is generally used for irrigation and livestock (Mace et al. 2001).

Capitan Reef Complex Aquifer. The Capitan Reef Complex Aquifer consists of Permian reef-derived
limestone and dolomite (Ryder 1996). Along the Culberson–Hudspeth County line within the project area,
the Capitan Reef Complex Aquifer is a confined to semi-confined carbonate aquifer. In areas along the
Culberson-Hudspeth County line (near the Project), the Capitan Reef Complex Aquifer is confined by more
than 2,000 feet of overlying Tertiary to Quaternary basin-fill, alluvium, and evaporite deposits. The Capitan
Reef Complex Aquifer is generally several hundred feet thick and may locally exceed 1,000 feet thick
(Standen et al. 2009). The aquifer is composed of massive to cavernous dolomite and limestone, and well
yields in Culberson and Hudspeth counties generally range from 400 gpm to more than 1,000 gpm (TWBD
2021). The depth to groundwater in the aquifer along the Culberson-Hudspeth County line generally ranges



DESERT SOUTHWEST EXPANSION PROJECT                   2                    TRANSWESTERN PIPELINE COMPANY, LLC
 RESOURCE REPORT 2                                     DRAFT                            WATER USE AND QUALITY



from approximately 100 to 200 feet bgs (Ryder 1996). The water quality is slightly saline to saline and
characterized by high TDS, and regionally it is used to irrigate salt-tolerant crops (George et al. 2011).

Bone Spring–Victorio Peak Aquifer. The Bone Spring–Victorio Peak Aquifer consists of fractured
Permian limestone, dolomite, and sandstone (Ryder 1996). The thickness of the Bone Spring–Victorio Peak
Aquifer is as much as 2,000 feet thick. Groundwater is generally unconfined where the aquifer is exposed
or shallow but may exhibit locally confined conditions where overlain by low-permeability strata. The
aquifer is locally highly transmissive. Well yield is highly variable due to joints, fractures, and solution
cavities in the formation and ranges from 150 gpm to more than 2,200 gpm (Ryder 1996). The depth to
groundwater ranges from a few feet bgs near salt flats and from approximately 30 feet bgs in the eastern
portion to greater than 300 feet bgs in the western portion of the irrigated region of the valley (Ashworth
2001). Groundwater quality ranges from slightly saline to moderately saline and is characterized by elevated
TDS, calcium, sulfate, and chloride concentrations from dissolved minerals and agricultural water
percolating through soluble minerals (Ashworth 2001). Most of the water is used for irrigation (99 percent
in 1985) (Ryder 1996).

2.2.1.2 Rio Grande Aquifer System – Lower Animas, Lordsburg, Mimbres, Mesilla Bolson, and
        Hueco Bolson Aquifers
The mainline (MPs 170 to 360) and the Red Chile Lateral cross areas underlain by the Rio Grande Aquifer
System, which extends across southern New Mexico and into far west Texas (USGS 2003). Principal basins
and aquifers traversed within this segment include, from east to west, the Hueco Bolson and the Mesilla,
Mimbres, Lower Animas, and Lordsburg Basins. Although the USGS Principal Aquifers map (USGS 2003)
classifies these basins as part of the Rio Grande Aquifer System, regional hydrogeologic investigations
indicate that the Mesilla Basin and Hueco Bolson are structurally and hydraulically associated with the Rio
Grande Rift, whereas the Mimbres, Lower Animas, and Lordsburg Basins are more consistent hydraulically
with internally drained Basin and Range basin-fill aquifers similar to those described in Section 2.2.1.3.
The New Mexico Office of the State Engineer (NMOSE) has established Declared Groundwater Basins for
groundwater administration and permitting. These administrative basin boundaries do not necessarily
correspond to hydrogeologic basin or aquifer boundaries described in published geologic investigations
(Hawley et al. 2025). For consistency with the groundwater management discussion presented in Section
2.2.4, the aquifer descriptions in this report are organized according to the applicable NMOSE Declared
Groundwater Basins where practical, while the hydrogeologic characterization is based on published
geologic and hydrogeologic investigations.

Aquifer materials within the Hueco Bolson and Mesilla Basin consist of Quaternary Rio Grande floodplain
alluvium underlain and laterally bounded by Tertiary and Quaternary Santa Fe Group basin-fill deposits
composed of fluvial, alluvial-fan, and basin-floor sediments (Nickerson and Myers 1993; Mack et al. 1984;
Hawley et al. 2025). Aquifer materials within the Mimbres, Lower Animas, and Lordsburg Basins of
western New Mexico consist primarily of unconsolidated to semi-consolidated Tertiary and Quaternary
basin-fill deposits, including alluvial-fan, stream-channel, playa, and fine-grained lacustrine and basin-axis
sediments (Hanson et al. 1994; Johnson and Rappuhn 2002).

Basin-fill thickness varies substantially across aquifers in the central segment. Basin-fill deposits locally
exceed 9,000 feet in the Hueco Bolson (Hawley et al. 2025), exceed approximately 2,000 feet in the Mesilla
Basin (Nickerson and Myers 1993), locally exceed 5,000 feet in the Mimbres Basin (Hanson et al. 1994),
and exceed several thousand feet in the structural centers of the Lower Animas and Lordsburg Basins
(Johnson and Rappuhn 2002). Saturated thickness varies with basin geometry, recharge, and pumping
history.

These studies indicate that groundwater within the basin-fill aquifer systems occurs under both unconfined
and confined conditions. Shallow groundwater is generally unconfined within coarse-grained alluvial-fan,
stream-channel, and Rio Grande alluvial deposits, particularly near basin margins and major drainages. At
greater depths, discontinuous to regionally extensive clay-rich lacustrine and basin-axis deposits locally
confine underlying sand and gravel aquifer units, resulting in semi-confined to confined groundwater
conditions within portions of the Hueco, Mesilla, Mimbres, Lower Animas, and Lordsburg basin-fill aquifer
systems. Depth to groundwater varies significantly depending on topography, recharge conditions, and
groundwater withdrawals. Groundwater is generally shallowest beneath floodplains, playas, and irrigated
agricultural areas, where water levels commonly occur within a few to several tens of feet bgs. In contrast,
groundwater beneath basin margins, mesas, piedmont areas, and municipal and agricultural pumping
centers commonly occurs at depths exceeding 100 feet bgs. Freshwater resources are generally concentrated
within the upper basin-fill aquifers and become progressively more saline with increasing depth and toward
basin centers.

Transmissivity is highly variable and is generally highest in coarse-grained basin-axis, buried-channel, and
Santa Fe Group sand and gravel deposits, and lowest where fine-grained basin-fill deposits dominate or
where aquifer intervals are separated by laterally extensive clay or silt. Reported hydraulic conductivity
values for central-segment aquifers span several orders of magnitude, typically ranging from approximately
1 to 200 ft/d, with locally higher values approaching 800 ft/d in coarse-grained deposits (Hanson et al. 1994;
Johnson and Rappuhn 2002; Nickerson and Myers 1993; Golab and AlKurdi 2025). Accordingly, well
yields are highly variable. Municipal and irrigation wells completed in the Hueco Bolson and Mesilla Basin
commonly yield more than 1,000 gpm and locally exceed 2,000 gpm where coarse Santa Fe Group and Rio
Grande alluvial deposits are present (Nickerson and Myers 1993; Mace et al. 2001). Farther west, irrigation
and municipal wells completed in the Mimbres, Lower Animas, and Lordsburg basin-fill aquifers
commonly yield several hundred gallons per minute, with locally higher yields where thick, coarse-grained
alluvial deposits are present (Hanson et al. 1994; Johnson and Rappuhn 2002). The New Mexico Office of
the State Engineer (NMOSE) well records primarily report permitted groundwater appropriations (acre-feet
per year) associated with water rights rather than demonstrated well-production capacities; therefore,
published hydrogeologic investigations were used to characterize regional well productivity.

Groundwater within the central segment provides municipal, irrigation, livestock, industrial, and domestic
water supplies. Based on review of available reports, regional groundwater quality is principally affected
by naturally elevated concentrations of total dissolved solids (TDS), hardness, sulfate, fluoride, arsenic, and
chloride associated with geochemical conditions in basin-fill sediments. Elevated nitrate concentrations
have also been documented in areas affected by agricultural activity and wastewater. In the Hueco Bolson
and Mesilla Basin, long-term groundwater withdrawals have resulted in localized migration of naturally
occurring brackish to saline groundwater into freshwater-producing zones (Anderholm and Heywood 2003;
Heywood and Yager 2003).

2.2.1.3 Basin and Range Basin-Fill Aquifers – Far West New Mexico and Arizona
The mainline (MPs 360 to 525) and nine laterals (Apache, Willcox, San Manuel, Saguaro, Germann, ED3,
Desert Sun, Harquahala, and Mojave Energy Park) cross areas underlain by the Basin and Range basin-fill
aquifers. The Basin and Range basin-fill aquifer systems developed within fault-bounded alluvial basins.
These aquifers consist primarily of unconsolidated to semi-consolidated alluvial-fan, stream-channel,
floodplain, basin-axis, and playa deposits (Robson and Banta 1995). Coarse-grained sand and gravel
deposits generally form the principal water-bearing zones, while clay-rich basin-center, lacustrine, and
playa deposits commonly function as local confining or semi-confining units. Regionally, the aquifers are
bounded by relatively low-permeability bedrock uplands that serve as recharge areas and structural controls
on groundwater flow (Robson and Banta 1995).

Basin-fill thickness is highly variable across the Arizona segment. Deposits are generally thinner along
bedrock margins and piedmont slopes and thicker toward basin centers. Reported basin-fill thicknesses
range from approximately 1,000 to 5,000 feet in many basins and may locally exceed 10,000 feet in
structurally deep basins in south-central Arizona (Robson and Banta 1995). The saturated thickness of
basin-fill aquifers varies with basin geometry, recharge, and groundwater withdrawals.

Depth to groundwater ranges from locally shallow conditions (few to tens of feet bgs) near large streams
and rivers, irrigated areas, and playas to more than several hundred feet bgs beneath upland piedmonts and
heavily pumped agricultural areas (ADWR 2026a, ADWR 2026b). Groundwater generally exists under
unconfined conditions within the basin aquifers; however, fine-grained playa, lacustrine, and alluvial
deposits that overlie coarser water-bearing deposits may produce perched, semi-confined, or locally
confined groundwater conditions. Deep semi-confined to confined aquifer conditions have been
documented in several southeastern Arizona basins, including the San Pedro, San Simon, and Willcox
basins (Anderson et al. 1992).

Transmissivity is generally highest where saturated coarse alluvial-fan, channel, and buried-stream deposits
are laterally connected and lowest in fine-grained playa, lacustrine, and alluvial deposits. Hydraulic
conductivity of basin-fill sediments spans several orders of magnitude depending on grain size and degree
of consolidation; representative values range from approximately 1 to 100 ft/d (Anderson et al. 1992).
Groundwater flow generally occurs from mountain-front recharge areas and bedrock uplands toward basin
axes, washes, playas, and local discharge zones (Anderson et al. 1992, Robertson 1991).

Well yields are highly variable and ADWR Groundwater Site Inventory (GWSI) data indicate that
municipal and irrigation wells within the Arizona Basin and Range commonly yield several hundred gpm,
with yields locally exceeding 2,000 gpm in the productive coarse-grained basin-fill aquifers (ADWR
2026a).

Groundwater resources within the Arizona Basin and Range basin-fill aquifers provide municipal,
irrigation, domestic, livestock, mining, and industrial water supplies. Water quality is generally more
favorable near recharge areas and less favorable in basin centers, playas, and areas affected by agricultural
return flow or evaporative concentration. Principal groundwater quality concerns include elevated TDS,
hardness, sulfate, fluoride, arsenic, and chloride resulting from prolonged hydrogeochemical processes in
closed or poorly-flushed basins, and anthropogenic inputs (volatile organic compounds [VOCs], nitrate)
from agricultural activity (Robertson 1991, Thiros et al. 2010). Individual Basin and Range basin-fill
aquifers are described in the following sections, from east to west.

San Simon Valley Sub-basin. The mainline (MPs 360 to 402.7) crosses the San Simon Valley Sub-basin
within Cochise County in southeastern Arizona. The basin extends northward into Graham County, Arizona
and eastward into Hidalgo County, New Mexico (ADWR 2015). Basin-fill deposits within the sub-basin
generally range from less than 1,000 feet thick along basin margins to more than 6,400 feet thick in the
structurally deep central portion of the basin between Bowie and Olga, in the vicinity of the Project (ADWR
2015). Basin-fill deposits consist of interbedded coarse- and fine-grained alluvial and basin-axis deposits.
In the vicinity of Bowie and San Simon areas (along the Project), local fine-grained units separate
unconfined shallow aquifers from a confined lower aquifer. Depth to groundwater near the Project generally
ranges from approximately 50 to more than 400 feet bgs (USGS 2023). Long-term agricultural groundwater
withdrawals, primarily concentrated in the Bowie–San Simon area, have produced regional water-level

and earth fissuring (ADWR 2015).Willcox Basin. The mainline (MPs 402.7 to 423.1) and the Apache

northward into Graham County (ADWR 2000). The basin is characterized by a large central playa (Willcox
Playa) surrounded by coarser alluvial-fan and stream-channel deposits. Basin-fill deposits within the sub-

The SSA comprises a complex sequence of unconsolidated to consolidated alluvial and basin-fill deposits
that form interconnected aquifer units within the Upper Santa Cruz Valley and Avra Valley sub-basins
(ADWR 2006, ADWR 2022a). Basin-fill thickness ranges from less than 1,000 feet thick along basin
margins to as much as 9,000 feet thick in the Avra Basin, and as much as 11,200 feet thick in the Upper
Santa Cruz Basin (ADWR 2006). The upper basin-fill unit ranges from several hundred feet to as much as
1,000 feet thick in both basins and generally consists of semi-consolidated to unconsolidated gravel, sands,
and silt. The lower basin-fill is several thousand feet thick and consists of conglomerates, gravels, sands,
silts, and mudstones. The saturated upper and lower basin-fill sediments form the regional aquifer system.
Groundwater in the regional aquifer is generally unconfined or partially confined to depths of about 1,000
feet bgs; localized confining conditions occur in fine-grained lower basin-fill deposits (ADWR 2006).

Historically, groundwater levels were relatively shallow in portions of the Upper Santa Cruz and Avra
Basins, particularly near the Santa Cruz River floodplain. However, sustained pumping through the mid-
to-late 20th century resulted in water-level declines exceeding 150 feet in areas (ADWR 2026). Based on
groundwater level data in the Arizona Groundwater Explorer, reported groundwater depths in the SSA near
the Project generally range from approximately 150 to more than 400 feet bgs (USGS 2023). Water-level
fluctuations reflect seasonal pumping cycles, natural recharge, and managed recharge operations, with
larger local fluctuations near active production wells and managed recharge facilities (ADWR 2022a).
ADWR GWSI data indicate that municipal and irrigation wells within the SSA commonly yield 500 gpm
or more (ADWR 2026a).

The Upper Santa Cruz & Avra Basin SSA supplies municipal, domestic, agricultural, and industrial users
within the Tucson AMA. The aquifer system is also used for managed recharge, storage, and recovery of
Central Arizona Project (CAP) water by the City of Tucson and other regional water providers (ADWR
2022a). Groundwater management and groundwater quality within the Tucson AMA are described in
Section 2.2.4.3.

2.2.4.2 New Mexico

are political subdivisions of the state established under the Soil and Water Conservation District Act
(NMSA 73-20-25 through 73-20-48). SWCDs coordinate with the New Mexico Department of Agriculture
(NMDA) and the NRCS to promote soil and water conservation, erosion control, flood and sediment
damage prevention, and wildlife preservation (NMDA 2026).

are administered by the NMOSE, GMAs in this report are based on NMOSE Declared Groundwater Basins.
These administrative boundaries provide the regulatory framework applicable to groundwater use along the

sections from east to west.

Temporary groundwater withdrawals associated with construction, if required, would be coordinated with
NMOSE to determine applicable permitting requirements. Transwestern understands that groundwater

1978, while any discharge of construction dewatering effluent would be subject to applicable water-quality
and stormwater permitting requirements administered by the New Mexico Environment Department
(NMED) and, where applicable, the EPA.

is hydraulically connected to the Rio Grande throughout much of the Mesilla Valley. Groundwater quality

mixing with deeper saline groundwater, while elevated nitrate has been documented beneath agricultural

groundwater flow patterns and is the primary driver of groundwater-level change (Johnson and Rappuhn

2.2.4.3 Arizona
Arizona enacted the Groundwater Management Code (GMC) in 1980 in response to groundwater
withdrawals that exceeded aquifer recharge in rapidly growing regions. The GMC, administered by ADWR,
established AMAs and a regulatory framework for protecting groundwater resources. The GMC requires
that ADWR develop a series of management plans for each AMA. Regulatory programs described in the
management plans include specific requirements for groundwater users, preconditions for well construction
and permitting, and conservation requirements applicable to agricultural, municipal, and industrial users.

The Project will not require long-term groundwater withdrawals; however, temporary groundwater
withdrawals associated with construction activities (e.g., localized dewatering, hydrostatic testing) may
require compliance with applicable state and AMA groundwater withdrawal and permitting requirements.

The Project is located within the boundaries of the Willcox, Tucson, Pinal, and Phoenix AMAs and the
Harquahala INA. Hydrogeologic and regulatory conditions within each boundary are described in the
following sections.

Willcox AMA. The mainline, between MPs 403 and 423, and the Apache Lateral cross the Willcox AMA,
which encompasses portions of Cochise and Graham counties in southeastern Arizona. The Willcox AMA
was established following decades of groundwater-level decline, land subsidence of up to 11.5 feet, and
earth fissure development caused primarily by agricultural groundwater withdrawals. ADWR is currently
preparing the initial management plan for the AMA (ADWR 2025).

GWSI data indicate that wells within the AMA have a reported average depth to water of 167 feet and an
average yield of 303 gpm (ADWR 2026a, ADWR 2026b).

A study completed in 1999 by the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality (ADEQ) reported
exceedances of EPA primary MCLs (standards that protect against contaminants that pose a risk to human

antimony. The study also reported exceedances of secondary MCL water quality standards in 23 of 58 wells
including fluoride, pH, chloride, and sulfate. According to the study, the reported exceedances of drinking
water standards within the Willcox AMA (with the exception of nitrate) are attributed to naturally-occurring
constituents in the local geology (ADEQ 2001).

2.2.8 Groundwater Construction and Operation Impacts and Mitigation
The primary construction activities that could affect groundwater are clearing of vegetation, excavation and
dewatering of the trench, soil mixing and compaction, and fuel and lubricant handling. Potential impacts
will be avoided or minimized by the use of standard construction techniques and adherence to
Transwestern’s FERC Procedures, Spill Prevention and Response (SPAR) Plan (see Appendix 2B), and
Groundwater Supply Monitoring and Mitigation Plan (see Appendix 2C).

Transwestern may use water obtained from local commercial or municipal water providers, surface water
rights owners, or from groundwater wells for dust suppression, construction, and hydrostatic testing.
Additional details regarding water use for construction activities are provided in Resource Report 1 and in
Section 2.4 below. The impacts to groundwater drawdown from any construction-related withdrawals will
be short-term. The long-term operational groundwater need for the compressor stations will be relatively
small for on-site facilities, and the pipeline and other aboveground facilities are not anticipated to require

2.2.8.1 Clearing
Clearing and grading can remove vegetation that acts as a filter or affects the groundwater recharge rate.
Vegetation will only be cleared where necessary, and vegetation will be allowed to re-establish (with the
exception of aboveground facility sites) upon completion of construction. Shallow aquifers could
experience minor impacts from changes in overland water flow and recharge caused by clearing and
grading, but these impacts are expected to be temporary and insignificant.

2.2.8.2 Trench Excavation and Dewatering
Trench excavation for the mainline and laterals will generally range from about 8 to 10 feet in depth, which
is typically too shallow to have a direct impact on the aquifer systems underlying the proposed construction
disturbance. Trench excavation will be too shallow and too narrow to alter groundwater flow or have a
significant effect on the major aquifer systems underlying the mainline and laterals. As indicated in
Resource Report 7, based on NRCS soil survey data, there are limited areas where shallow groundwater
(i.e., 60 inches or less) may occur along the Project. These areas are associated with the Pecos River Valley
and Salt Basin (playa) in Texas, the Rio Grande River crossing in New Mexico, and Bass and Wildcat
canyons in Arizona. If dewatering is necessary to allow access to the trench, pumping of groundwater may
occur where there is shallow groundwater. The potential effect of groundwater withdrawal on aquifer users
will depend on the rate and duration of pumping. Construction activities within a particular location are
typically completed within several days, and any lowering of the groundwater table is expected to be
temporary and localized. Transwestern will minimize the amount of time the trench remains open to allow
the water table to return to original elevations as soon as practicable.

If dewatering is necessary, in order to recharge the aquifer and prevent silt-laden waters from flowing into
nearby waterbodies, Transwestern proposes to discharge all water from dewatering activities into upland
areas using straw bale dewatering structures or silt bags as described in the Erosion Control and
Revegetation Plan (ECRP, Appendix 1G to Resource Report 1). Dewatering activities will be coordinated
with appropriate regional regulators. Implementation of these procedures is expected to minimize the
impact on groundwater during dewatering operations. Project field surveys identified no springs and only
two wetlands (associated with the Pecos River/MP 31.33 and Salt Creek/MP 43.74 crossing in Texas). To
avoid potential impacts to the Pecos River and Salt Creek and the adjacent wetlands, they will be crossed
by trenchless methods. Transwestern will follow Transwestern’s FERC Procedures, requiring the use of
trench breakers or installation of trench plugs at the edges of waterbodies/dry washes and on slopes. Trench
plugs are installed after the pipeline is installed in the trench and prior to trench backfilling.

To avoid long-term changes in water table elevation and subsurface hydrology, excavated surface soils and
subsoils would be segregated, where appropriate, and returned as nearly as practicable to their original soil
horizon. With the use of these measures, significant impacts to groundwater pathways are not likely.

Because construction activity is generally limited to surface disturbance and shallow trenching is temporary
and contained within the approved construction work areas, groundwater wells (both public and private)
beyond 200 feet of the construction work areas are not expected to be affected by the Project. Pre-

2.2.8.6 Fuel Handling
Groundwater contamination could occur from an inadvertent spill of fuels, lubricants, and other materials
used during construction. Implementation of proper storage, containment, and handling procedures will
minimize the chance of such releases. Prompt cleanup responses will prevent migration of contaminants
to the groundwater. Transwestern’s SPAR Plan (see Appendix 2B) describes measures which will be
implemented to prevent and control inadvertent spills of hazardous materials. These measures include, but
are not limited to:

   •    prohibiting fueling, lubricating and hazardous material storage in or adjacent to sensitive areas
        shown on the alignment sheets (see Appendix 1B-1 and Appendix 1B-2 to Resource Report 1);
   •    implementing trench dewatering procedures to prevent contamination (such as using pump
        containment structures and equipment inspection);
   •    specifying collection and disposal procedures for wastes generated during equipment
        maintenance;
   •    utilizing emergency response procedures; and
   •    developing standard procedures for excavation and off-site disposal of any soils contaminated by
        spillage.

Prior to construction, implementation of the SPAR Plan will identify the types and quantities of hazardous
materials that will be stored/used during construction. Personnel will be trained and prepared to implement
the SPAR Plan.

Equipment fueling and storage of fuel, oil, and other fluids during construction could create a potential
long-term contamination hazard to aquifers. Hazardous liquid spills or leaks could contaminate
groundwater and affect aquifer users. Soil contamination could continue to add pollutants to the
groundwater long after a spill has occurred. This type of impact will be avoided or minimized by restricting
the location of fueling and hazardous material storage and by requiring immediate cleanup in the event of
a spill or leak. Transwestern will prohibit fueling activities and storage of hazardous materials within 200
feet of all private water supply wells and within 400 feet of all public supply wells unless implemented in
accordance with the SPAR Plan. Following the implementation of the SPAR Plan and mitigation measures,
impacts to groundwater resources are expected to be reduced to less than significant levels.

2.3     SURFACE WATER RESOURCES

This section describes the surface water resources crossed or potentially affected by the Project. Information
presented includes regulatory jurisdictions, the types and distribution of existing surface water features,
identification of any sensitive or protected surface waters, and a summary of measures proposed to avoid,
minimize, and/or mitigate potential effects associated with construction and operation of the Project.

2.3.1 Regulatory Jurisdiction
The Project is subject to FERC requirements for waterbody and wetland crossings, as well as the U.S. Army
Corps of Engineers (USACE) and applicable state and local regulations. Regulatory authority, permitting
requirements, and resource protection measures vary depending on how surface water features are defined
and regulated by the applicable jurisdiction. The following sections summarize the principal regulatory
authorities applicable to surface water resources crossed by the Project.

2.3.1.1 Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
FERC’s Procedures define a waterbody as:

        “Any natural or artificial stream, river, or drainage with perceptible flow at the time of crossing,
        and other permanent waterbodies such as ponds and lakes.”

Although FERC does not determine Clean Water Act jurisdiction, it establishes construction, restoration,
and mitigation requirements for waterbodies crossed by natural gas pipelines, subject to its regulations.
Construction and mitigation measures applicable to Project waterbody crossings will be implemented in
accordance with Transwestern’s FERC Procedures and the best management practices (BMPs) described
in this Resource Report and Resource Report 1.

2.3.1.2 U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
Pursuant to Section 404 of the Clean Water Act (33 United States Code [U.S.C.] §1344), the USACE
regulates the discharge of dredged or fill material into Waters of the United States (WOTUS), including
jurisdictional wetlands. As defined in 33 CFR §328.3, and as applicable to the Project, WOTUS may
include traditional navigable waters, interstate waters, relatively permanent tributaries to those waters,
certain impoundments, and adjacent wetlands that maintain a continuous surface connection to
jurisdictional waters (USACE and EPA 2025).

As provided in Appendix 1I to Resource Report 1, authorization for Project activities affecting jurisdictional
waters is anticipated to be obtained through USACE Nationwide Permit 12, Utility Line Activities, or other
authorization as determined through coordination with the USACE.

2.3.1.3 State of Texas – Water in the State
Texas regulates “water in the state” pursuant to TWC §26.001. These waters include groundwater and a
broad range of surface water resources, including rivers, streams, creeks, lakes, reservoirs, wetlands,
marshes, estuaries, and other natural or artificial waterbodies, regardless of navigability.

Surface water resources are protected through programs administered by the TCEQ, including surface water
quality standards, pollutant discharge permitting, and other water quality protection requirements.

2.3.1.4 State of New Mexico – Waters of the State
Under the New Mexico Water Quality Act, “waters ” are defined as all surface and groundwater, whether
natural or artificial, public or private, except water confined and retained completely upon the property of

The New Mexico Environment Department (NMED) through the Water Quality Control Commission
(WQCC) administers water quality protections through the New Mexico Water Quality Act and state water
quality standards established to protect designated beneficial uses of surface waters (NMED 2025).
2.3.1.5 State of Arizona – Waters of the State
Arizona defines “waters of the state” under Arizona Revised Statutes §49-201(50) to include all waters
within the jurisdiction of the state, including perennial and intermittent streams, lakes, ponds, reservoirs,
marshes, watercourses, waterways, wells, aquifers, springs, irrigation systems, drainage systems, and other
natural or artificial surface and subsurface waters.

Arizona’s definition of waters of the state is broader than the federal definition of WOTUS. The Arizona
Surface Water Protection Program (SWPP) protects WOTUS as well as additional surface waters identified
on the Protected Surface Waters List (PSWL). Surface water quality standards established by the state apply
to waters regulated under the SWPP.

2.3.1.6 County Waters – Pima and Pinal Counties, Arizona
Certain counties crossed by the Project maintain additional regulations or guidance related to riparian
resources associated with washes, streams, and other surface water features.
In Pima County, Ordinance 16.30 establishes requirements for the protection of watercourses and riparian
habitats (Pima 2026). The County has mapped regulated riparian habitat, including hydroriparian,
mesoriparian, xeroriparian, and important riparian habitat classifications. Activities involving vegetation
clearing or disturbance within mapped riparian areas may require a Floodplain Use Permit or other county
authorization.
Pinal County has developed riparian area management guidelines intended to identify, protect, and
minimize impacts on riparian resources throughout the county (Pinal County 2026). Although these
guidelines are non-regulatory, they provide recommendations that may be considered during Project
planning and permitting activities.

2.3.2 Watersheds
The EPA defines a watershed as an area of land in which all precipitation and surface runoff drain to a
common receiving waterbody, such as a stream, river, lake, wetland, estuary, or ocean (EPA 2026d).
Watersheds represent natural hydrologic boundaries and are commonly used to organize and evaluate
surface water resources. Watersheds crossed by the Project were identified using the USGS Watershed
Boundary Dataset (WBD), which delineates hydrologic units across the United States based on surface
drainage patterns and watershed divides. The WBD assigns each watershed a Hydrologic Unit Code (HUC)
that allows for standardized identification and analysis of drainage basins. The Project is located within 26
HUC 8 watersheds (see Tables 2.3-1 and 2.3-2).

2.3.3 Waterbodies
Transwestern conducted field surveys for surface water resources between December 2025 and June 2026.
Surveys were conducted in accordance with the methodologies described in the applicable aquatic resource
survey reports. The aquatic survey report for Texas is included in Appendix 3B to Resource Report 3, and
aquatic survey reports for New Mexico and Arizona are included in Appendix 2D-1 and Appendix 2D-2,
respectively. Prior to field investigations, Transwestern conducted a desktop review of National Wetlands
Inventory (NWI) and National Hydrography Dataset (NHD) data, USGS topographic mapping, and
available aerial imagery to identify potential surface water resources within and adjacent to the project area.

Field surveys were conducted within an approximate 400-foot-wide Environmental Survey Area (ESA),
consisting of approximately 80 feet on one side of the centerline and 320 feet on the opposite side. The
narrower portion of the ESA generally paralleled existing pipeline or other linear infrastructure where
present. Surface water features in locations that were inaccessible during field surveys were identified
through desktop interpretation of topographic mapping, aerial imagery, and other available geospatial
datasets.

For purposes of environmental review, FERC classifies waterbodies according to width as follows:

    •   Major Waterbodies: greater than 100 feet wide
    •   Intermediate Waterbodies: greater than 10 feet wide and less than or equal to 100 feet wide
    •   Minor Waterbodies: less than or equal to 10 feet wide
Waterbody width classifications presented in this report are based on the FERC criteria. Consistent with
FERC guidance, waterbody classifications are used to evaluate potential construction impacts and identify
applicable mitigation measures.

2.3.3.1 Mainline and Laterals
The Project will cross perennial, intermittent, ephemeral, and open waterbodies as well as artificial
conveyances. Perennial waterbodies flow or contain standing water year-round and are typically capable of
supporting populations of fish and macroinvertebrates. Intermittent waterbodies flow or contain standing
water seasonally and are typically dry for part of the year. Ephemeral waterbodies generally contain water
only in response to precipitation. Open water consists of large pond or lake systems. Artificial conveyances
consist of canals and ditches where the flow regime is a result of flooding controlled by pumps, siphons,
dikes, or dams. Only two perennial waterbodies are crossed by the Project (both by HDD): the Pecos
River/MP 31.31 and Salt Creek/MP 43.74, both in Reeves County, Texas.

Ephemeral waterbodies crossed by the Project consist primarily of dry washes, arroyos, and desert washes,
which are common throughout the project area. These features convey runoff only in response to
precipitation events and generally lack sustained baseflow. While flow durations are typically brief, storm
events may generate substantial localized runoff and sediment transport. Of the 928 waterbodies crossed
by the mainline and laterals, approximately 790 (85 percent) are classified as ephemeral or intermittent
(including the Rio Grande, San Pedro River, and Big Wash). Project design and restoration practices will
maintain the hydraulic function of these features and minimize impacts to natural drainage patterns. The
waterbodies affected by the mainline and laterals, including attributes and proposed crossing methods, are
provided in Table 2A-6 in Appendix 2A. Table 2.3-3 and Table 2.3-4 provide a summary of the waterbodies
crossed by the mainline and laterals based on FERC’s width criteria, using field observations of channel
morphology, flow characteristics, and ordinary high-water indicators.

2.3.4 Water Quality Classifications
Water quality standards establish the regulatory framework for protecting surface water resources and are
a fundamental component of the water quality-based pollution control programs implemented under the
Clean Water Act (CWA). Water quality standards consist of designated uses, water quality criteria
established to protect those uses, and antidegradation policies intended to maintain and protect existing
water quality. Pursuant to Section 303(c) of the CWA, states are responsible for adopting and periodically
reviewing water quality standards for waters within their jurisdiction.

2.3.4.1 Texas Water Quality Classifications
The TCEQ is responsible for administering water quality standards and designating use classifications for
surface waters in Texas. These standards are codified in the Texas Surface Water Quality Standards
(TSWQS) at 30 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) Chapter 307. TCEQ assigns designated uses and water
quality criteria to classified stream segments, reservoirs, bays, and estuaries. Smaller tributaries, ephemeral
drainages, and other unclassified waters are protected under statewide water quality standards rather than
segment-specific criteria.

The primary Project waterbody crossing in Texas that is designated as a classified TCEQ stream segment
is the Pecos River (Segment 2311) in the Lower Pecos-Red Bluff Reservoir Basin near MP 31.31. The
designated uses for this segment include primary contact recreation and limited aquatic life use. This
crossing is proposed as an HDD to avoid impacts.

    2.3.5.5 Impaired Surface Waters
    The CWA establishes a framework for assessing and restoring waters that do not meet applicable water
    quality standards. Under Section 305(b) of the CWA, states are required to periodically assess the condition
    of their surface waters and submit an Integrated Report to the EPA. These reports evaluate the extent to

which surface waters support their designated uses and identify waters that are impaired or threatened.
Under Section 303(d) of the CWA and implementing regulations at 40 CFR Section 130.7, states must
identify waters that are not expected to attain water quality standards after implementation of technology-
based controls and prioritize those waters for development of Total Maximum Daily Loads (TMDLs). A
TMDL establishes the maximum amount of a pollutant that a waterbody can receive while continuing to
meet applicable water quality standards and support its designated uses.

Surface water quality standards applicable to Project waterbodies are administered by the respective state
regulatory agencies. In Texas, the TCEQ develops and administers the Texas Surface Water Quality
Standards codified at 30 TAC Chapter 307 (TCEQ 2022). In New Mexico, the NMED Surface Water
Quality Bureau administers the water quality standards contained in NMAC 20.6.4, Standards for Interstate
and Intrastate Surface Waters (NMED 2026c). In Arizona, the ADEQ administers the Arizona Surface
Water Quality Standards set forth in AAC Title 18, Chapter 11.

Integrated Reports and Impaired Waters
Biennially, Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona prepare Integrated Reports pursuant to Sections 305(b) and
303(d) of the CWA. These reports evaluate the attainment status of assessed waters and identify waters that
do not meet applicable water quality standards. Waterbodies are evaluated relative to their designated uses
and are typically classified as fully supporting, fully supporting but threatened, partially supporting, or not
supporting those uses. Waters that do not fully support one or more designated uses are considered impaired.
States are also required to develop TMDLs for impaired waterbodies where pollutant reductions are
necessary to restore designated uses. Integrated Reports include assessment methodologies, water quality
assessment results, and lists of waters requiring TMDLs pursuant to Section 303(d) of the CWA. EPA
reviews and approves state-submitted impairment listings and associated TMDLs.

The most recent available Integrated Reports, Section 303(d) impaired waters lists, and associated GIS
datasets were reviewed to identify impaired waters, assessment units, and waters requiring TMDLs crossed
by or located near the Project. Sources reviewed include the TCEQ Integrated Report and Surface Water
Quality Viewer, the NMED Integrated Report and assessment databases, and ADEQ Integrated Assessment
and Listing Program resources.

Integrated Reports generally assign assessed waters to the following assessment categories:

    •   Category 1 – All designated uses are attained.
    •   Category 2 – Some designated uses are attained and insufficient information is available for other
        uses.
    •   Category 3 – Insufficient data are available to determine attainment status.
    •   Category 3A – Available information indicates a potential concern, but existing data are insufficient
        to support assignment to another category.
    •   Category 4 – Water quality standards are not attained, but development of a TMDL is not required.
        This category includes:
    •   Category 4A – A TMDL has been approved.
    •   Category 4B – Other pollution control requirements are expected to result in attainment of water
        quality standards.
    •   Category 4C – Impairment is not caused by a pollutant (e.g., altered flow conditions).
    •   Category 5 – Water quality standards are not attained and a TMDL is required.

Executive Order (EO) 11988, Floodplain Management, directs federal agencies to avoid, to the extent
practicable, adverse short- and long-term impacts associated with the occupancy and modification of
floodplains and to avoid direct or indirect support of floodplain development where a practicable alternative
exists. For the purposes of this assessment, floodplain information was obtained for New Mexico (excluding

Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMs) and associated National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL) data (FEMA 2026a

FEMA FIRMs do not provide coverage for the project area within Winkler, Loving, Reeves, Culberson,

ephemeral drainages, arroyos, desert washes, alluvial fans, playas, and localized flash flooding resulting
from high-intensity precipitation events. In mountainous areas of Culberson, Hudspeth, and El Paso
counties, rapid runoff from steep terrain may generate significant flood flows within normally dry channels.
The TWDB’s State Flood Plan identifies one percent annual chance floodplains, 0.2 percent annual chance

playa flooding, and localized flood hazards as significant considerations for flood risk assessment.

2.3.7 Construction Impacts and Mitigation
Surface water impacts associated with the Project may be either direct or indirect. Direct impacts occur
where construction activities temporarily or permanently affect a surface water feature within the approved
construction workspace. Indirect impacts may occur outside the construction workspace and can include
temporary changes in water quality resulting from sediment transport, stormwater runoff, or the inadvertent
release of construction-related materials.

Construction activities associated with the Project that have the potential to affect surface waters include
clearing activities, open-cut crossings of waterbodies, HDD or other trenchless crossings, hydrostatic test
discharges, potential spills or leaks of hazardous liquids from the refueling of construction vehicles or
storage of fuel, oil, and other fluids, and temporary access road crossings. Periodic maintenance of the
rights-of-way also has the potential to impact bank and riparian areas adjacent to waterbodies. These
impacts are expected to be localized and primarily limited to the construction period.

Stormwater runoff from construction work areas could result in the transport of sediment to adjacent

2.3.7.1 Waterbody Crossings
Waterbodies crossed by the Project and the proposed crossing methods are provided in Table 2A-6 in
Appendix 2A. All waterbody crossings will be constructed in accordance with Transwestern’s FERC
Procedures. The crossing methods are based on site-specific resource considerations, waterbody
characteristics, engineering constraints, and the objective of minimizing impacts on aquatic resources and
water quality. Figures for HDD crossings and a crossing plan for the Lordsburg Playa are provided in
Appendix 2E and Appendix 2F, respectively.

The majority of waterbody crossings consist of ephemeral washes, intermittent drainages, and artificial
conveyances that are expected to be dry at the time of construction. For ephemeral and non-flowing
intermittent waterbodies, Transwestern will generally utilize conventional upland construction techniques
in accordance with Transwestern’s FERC Procedures (see Appendix 1G to Resource Report 1). Where
water is present during construction, dry crossing methods, such as flume crossings, dam-and-pump
systems, or other approved flow diversion techniques, will be utilized as appropriate to maintain
downstream flow and minimize disturbance to aquatic resources. Major waterbodies and other
environmentally sensitive crossings will be crossed using trenchless methods, where practicable. Additional
details regarding waterbody crossing methods are provided in Resource Report 1.

Construction across rivers, streams, washes, canals, and other surface waters can result in temporary
impacts on water quality and aquatic resources if not properly managed. Potential construction-related
impacts include temporary increases in turbidity and sedimentation resulting from streambank disturbance,
trench excavation, and restoration activities. Surface runoff and erosion from disturbed areas may also
contribute sediment to adjacent waterbodies during construction. Mobile aquatic organisms, such as fish,
are generally expected to avoid localized areas temporarily affected by construction; however, less mobile
aquatic organisms may be affected by short-term changes in water quality. Potential effects on fisheries
resources and aquatic habitats are discussed further in Resource Report 3.

Long-term impacts on water quality and aquatic habitat could occur if disturbed streambanks and riparian
vegetation are not adequately restored following construction. Soil erosion, streambank instability, and loss
of riparian vegetation can contribute sediment to surface waters and affect aquatic habitat quality. To
minimize these potential long-term effects, disturbed streambeds, streambanks, and riparian areas will be
restored as closely as practicable to preconstruction contours and conditions in accordance with
Transwestern’s FERC Procedures. Vegetation clearing within riparian areas will be limited to the minimum
area necessary to safely construct, operate, and maintain the Project.

Potential impacts may also result from accidental releases of fuels, lubricants, hydraulic fluids, or other
hazardous materials during equipment operation, maintenance, or refueling. Long-term operational impacts
are expected to be limited primarily to periodic vegetation maintenance within the permanent right-of-way
at waterbody crossings. As such activities will be conducted in accordance with the procedures described
in the ECRP and applicable permit requirements, long-terms impacts will be reduced to less than significant
levels.

2.3.7.6 Floodplains
Construction within floodplain areas is generally unavoidable because many surface water crossings,
drainage features, and existing utility corridors occur within mapped flood-prone areas. As discussed in
Section 2.3.6, the Project crosses numerous FEMA, TWDB, and EDAC-mapped floodplain areas, including
Zones A, AE, and AO (see Tables 2.3-9, 2.3-10, and 2.3-11 and Table 2A-7 in Appendix 2A).

Temporary impacts on floodplain functions may occur during construction as a result of vegetation clearing,
grading, trench excavation, spoil storage, equipment operation, and restoration activities within the
construction workspace. These activities could temporarily affect floodwater storage, floodwater
conveyance, and localized drainage patterns. However, such impacts are expected to be localized,
temporary, and limited to the construction period.

To minimize impacts on floodplain resources, Transwestern will implement the measures contained in
Transwestern’s FERC Plan and Procedures, including erosion and sediment control BMPs, restoration of
preconstruction contours, stabilization of disturbed soils, and revegetation of disturbed areas. Following
pipeline installation, disturbed floodplain areas will be restored to preconstruction contours to the extent
practicable.

Several major waterbodies within mapped floodplains will be crossed using HDD methods (i.e., Pecos
River, Salt Creek, Rio Grande, San Pedro River, CAP Canal, Florence Canal, and Florence Casa Grande
Canal), which will avoid impacts within floodplain areas.

Following restoration, the buried mainline and laterals are not expected to impede flood flows, reduce flood
storage capacity, or substantially alter existing drainage patterns. Long-term operation of the Project is,
therefore, not expected to adversely affect floodplain values or functions.

Aboveground facilities located within mapped floodplains will be identified during final engineering design
and evaluated for consistency with applicable federal, state, and local floodplain management requirements.
As necessary, Transwestern will coordinate with the appropriate floodplain administrators and incorporate
floodplain considerations into final facility design. Site grading, drainage facilities, and stormwater
management features will be designed to maintain existing drainage patterns to the extent practicable and
minimize impacts on floodplain functions.

Although portions of the Project occur within mapped FEMA floodplain areas, construction-related impacts
are expected to be temporary. With implementation of the proposed mitigation measures and restoration
activities, the Project is not expected to cause significant long-term impacts on floodplain resources, flood
storage capacity, flood conveyance, or floodplain function.

To protect the buried mainline and laterals during operation, an evaluation of the risks associated with scour
and migration will be completed (see Appendix 6A to Resource Report 6) and appropriate mitigation
measures implemented.

2.3.7.7 Spills
Accidental spills or releases of fuels, lubricants, hydraulic fluids, drilling fluids, or other hazardous
materials used during construction could adversely affect surface water resources if they occur within or
adjacent to waterbodies, wetlands, drainage features, or floodplains. Potential spill sources include
equipment fueling and maintenance activities, fuel storage areas, material transport, and operation of
construction equipment. Although the likelihood of a spill is low, Transwestern will implement measures
to avoid and minimize the potential for impacts on surface water resources during construction.

Transwestern will implement the SPAR Plan, which establishes procedures for the handling, storage,
containment, reporting, and cleanup of hazardous materials. In accordance with Transwestern’s FERC
Procedures, hazardous materials, fuels, lubricants, and chemical products will generally be stored in upland
areas at least 100 feet from waterbodies and wetlands where practicable. Similarly, equipment fueling,
maintenance, and servicing activities will not occur within 100 feet of waterbodies or wetlands except
where necessary for safety, engineering, or environmental protection purposes.

Spill response equipment and materials will be maintained at active construction areas, and Project
personnel will be trained in spill prevention, containment, notification, and cleanup procedures. In the event
of a spill, Transwestern will immediately implement appropriate containment and response measures to
prevent the migration of contaminants to adjacent surface waters and will notify applicable regulatory
agencies, as required.

Additional precautions will be implemented at sensitive waterbody crossings, impaired waters, HDD
crossings, and other environmentally sensitive areas. Any inadvertent return associated with HDD
operations will be managed in accordance with Project-specific HDD contingency procedures (see
Appendix 2G) and applicable permit requirements.

With implementation of the SPAR Plan, adherence to Transwestern’s FERC Procedures, and application
of Project-specific BMPs, the risk of impacts to surface water resources from accidental spills is expected
to be low. Any impacts associated with a spill would be expected to be localized and temporary and would
be minimized through prompt containment, cleanup, and site restoration activities.

2.3.8 Operation Impacts and Mitigation
Routine operation and maintenance activities for the Project will primarily consist of periodic inspection,
integrity management, minimal vegetation maintenance, and repair activities within the permanent right-
of-way. Vegetation management activities may include selective clearing or mowing within the maintained
right-of-way and will be conducted in accordance with Transwestern’s FERC Procedures. Vegetation
maintenance will be limited to that necessary to support safe operation, integrity inspections, and regulatory
compliance and is not expected to result in significant adverse impacts on surface water resources, water
quality, wetlands, or riparian areas.

Following construction and restoration, the mainline and laterals will remain buried beneath streambeds,
washes, canals, and other surface water features crossed by the Project (see Appendix 6A to Resource
Report 6 for the scour and migration evaluation). As a result, operation of the Project is not expected to
affect surface water flow, channel morphology, sediment transport processes, flood conveyance, or aquatic
habitat conditions. Long-term impacts on hydrology, water quality, and waterbody function are therefore
not anticipated.

Operation of aboveground facilities is not expected to result in routine discharges to surface waters.
Stormwater runoff from developed facility areas will be managed in accordance with applicable federal,
state, and local regulations and site-specific drainage and stormwater management designs. Routine

2.4     WATER USE REQUIREMENTS

Water will be required during construction for activities such as hydrostatic testing, HDDs, and dust
suppression. Preliminary construction water sources and estimated water volumes are identified in Resource
Report 1. As currently planned, water for construction activities may be obtained from municipal water
systems, commercial water suppliers, purchased from surface water rights owners, groundwater sources, or
other legally available sources, subject to landowner approval and applicable permitting requirements.
Water sourcing plans, withdrawal locations, and final water use requirements will continue to be refined as
Project engineering and construction planning progress.

Hydrostatic test water will contact only newly constructed pipeline facilities and associated appurtenances.
Based on current Project planning, hydrostatic testing is not anticipated to require chemical additives,
biocides, corrosion inhibitors, or other treatment chemicals.

Following completion of hydrostatic testing, test water will be managed in accordance with Transwestern’s
FERC Plan and Procedures, and applicable federal, state, and local permit requirements. Where hydrostatic
test water is discharged to upland areas, appropriate energy dissipation devices, sediment controls, and other
BMPs will be implemented to minimize erosion, sediment transport, and impacts on adjacent resources.
Final discharge locations and discharge methods will be identified during detailed engineering and
permitting. Water used for HDD operations will primarily consist of water and bentonite-based drilling
fluid. HDD activities will be conducted in accordance with Project-specific HDD procedures, permit

conducted in accordance with the methodologies described in the applicable aquatic resource survey reports
included in Appendix 2D-1 (New Mexico), Appendix 2D-2 (Arizona) and Appendix 3B to Resource Report

conducted within an approximately 400-foot-wide ESA, consisting of approximately 80 feet on one side of
the Project centerline and 320 feet on the opposite side. The narrower portion of the ESA generally

2.5.2 Construction Impacts and Mitigation
The Pecos River and Salt Creek crossings, including their associated wetlands, are proposed to be
constructed using HDD methods. HDD installation allows the pipeline to be installed beneath the waterbody
and associated wetland resources without direct excavation within the wetland. As a result, direct impacts
on wetland vegetation, wetland soils, wetland hydrology, and wetland habitat are expected to be avoided at
these locations.

Although HDD construction avoids direct disturbance within wetlands, indirect impacts could occur if an
inadvertent return of drilling fluid were to reach a wetland area. To minimize this risk, HDD entry and exit
locations have been sited outside wetland boundaries, and HDD activities will be conducted in accordance
with Project-specific HDD procedures and contingency measures. Transwestern will implement monitoring
procedures during drilling activities and will maintain equipment and materials necessary to contain and
respond to any inadvertent return. In the event of an inadvertent return, Transwestern will implement
corrective actions consistent with the FERC Guidance for Horizontal Directional Drill Monitoring,
Inadvertent Return Response, and Contingency Plans and applicable permit requirements.

Temporary wetland impacts are not anticipated and no permanent loss of wetland acreage or long-term
impacts on wetland hydrology are anticipated as a result of Project construction.

Accidental releases of fuels, lubricants, hydraulic fluids, drilling fluids, or other hazardous materials could
adversely affect wetland resources if not properly managed. To minimize this risk, Transwestern will
implement its SPAR Plan. Hazardous materials will generally be stored in upland areas, equipment
refueling and servicing will be conducted away from wetlands, and spill response materials will be
maintained at active construction areas. Any releases will be promptly contained and remediated in
accordance with applicable regulatory requirements. With implementation of the HDD crossing designs,
Transwestern’s FERC Plan and Procedures, the SPAR Plan, and applicable permit conditions, impacts on
wetlands are expected to be avoided.

2.5.3 Operation Impacts and Mitigation
Wetlands will not be impacted because maintenance will not occur within the permanent easement
associated with HDD (or trenchless) crossings without prior regulatory approval. Maintenance activities
during operations will be conducted in accordance with Transwestern’s FERC Plan and Procedures and
SPAR Plan. Vegetation maintenance will be limited to that necessary to ensure safe operation and integrity
of the mainline and laterals and is not expected to affect the wetlands associated with the Pecos River and
Salt Creek HDD crossings.

With implementation of Transwestern’s FERC Procedures, the SPAR Plan, and applicable permit
conditions, no impacts on wetland resources are anticipated as a result of Project operation.

2.5.4 Wetland Crossing Permits
Any Project construction and operation activities that would result in a discharge of fill material into
federally jurisdictional wetlands would require compliance with applicable federal regulations, primarily
those of the USACE under Section 404 of the CWA. Although direct impacts on wetlands are not
anticipated, the Project's wetland crossings and associated construction activities will be reviewed and
coordinated with the USACE as part of the federal permitting process. Based on the currently proposed
HDD crossing designs, which avoid impacts to these wetlands, no USACE authorization of Project
activities at these wetlands is anticipated to be necessary. The Project will also comply with applicable
state requirements related to wetlands and water quality in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona.

2.5.5 Compensatory Wetland Mitigation
Because the identified wetlands will be crossed using HDD methods and no direct wetland impacts are
currently anticipated, compensatory wetland mitigation is not anticipated. The Project will not result in a
permanent loss of wetland acreage, permanent alteration of wetland hydrology, or conversion of wetland
vegetation communities.
