1.0         Introduction
Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC (Transwestern), a wholly-owned subsidiary of Energy Transfer LP
(Energy Transfer), is seeking authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or
Commission) pursuant to Section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act (NGA) to construct, own, and operate the
proposed Desert Southwest Expansion Project (DSWE Project or Project). The Project is an expansion of
the existing Transwestern system that will consist of approximately 525.2 miles of 48-inch diameter
mainline pipeline (mainline) and approximately 180.0 miles associated with 13 lateral pipelines (laterals),
as well as new compressor stations, associated meter stations, and other aboveground facilities located
in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. The Project will provide firm transportation service of up to 2.3 billion
cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) of natural gas from the Permian Basin to delivery points serving customers in
New Mexico and Arizona and will upgrade Transwestern’s existing Phoenix Lateral to allow bi-directional
flow.
The Project location in New Mexico is portrayed in Figure 1.
WESTECH Environmental Services, Inc. (WESTECH) was contracted to Transwestern to survey and
delineate aquatic resources along the Project that may require permitting and/or particular construction
and mitigation measures. This report documents desktop analysis and field surveys that were completed
to identify, delineate, and map aquatic resources along the proposed Project route in New Mexico, with
the exception of the Red Chile Lateral which was completed by On Pointe Consulting, LLC and which is
reported separately.

1.1 Definitions
The following sections define the types of features that were surveyed in this report.

        Waters of the United States
Waters of the United States (WOTUS) are defined in 33 C.F.R. § 328.3 (a) as the following:

        (a) Waters of the United States means:
         (1) Waters which are:
             (i) Currently used, or were used in the past, or may be susceptible to use in interstate
             or foreign commerce, including all waters which are subject to the ebb and flow of
             the tide;
             (ii) The territorial seas; or
             (iii) Interstate waters;
        (2) Impoundments of waters otherwise defined as waters of the United States under this
        definition, other than impoundments of waters identified under paragraph (a)(5) of this
        section;



                                                   2
                                                                      EXP Energy Services, Inc.
                                            DSW Aquatic Resource Inventory Report: New Mexico
                                                                                     July 2026



Figure 1. New Mexico Project Location




                                        3
                                                                                    EXP Energy Services, Inc.
                                                          DSW Aquatic Resource Inventory Report: New Mexico
                                                                                                   July 2026



        (3) Tributaries of waters identified in paragraph (a)(1) or (2) of this section that are
        relatively permanent, standing or continuously flowing bodies of water;
        (4) Wetlands adjacent to the following waters:
             (i) Waters identified in paragraph (a)(1) of this section; or(ii) Relatively permanent,
             standing or continuously flowing bodies of water identified in paragraph (a)(2) or
             (a)(3) of this section and with a continuous surface connection to those waters;
        (5) Intrastate lakes and ponds not identified in paragraphs (a)(1) through (4) of this section
        that are relatively permanent, standing or continuously flowing bodies of water with a
        continuous surface connection to the waters identified in paragraph (a)(1) or (a)(3) of this
        section.

1.2 Waters of the State: New Mexico
The state of New Mexico has a more expansive definition of waters of the State compared to the definition
of WOTUS. New Mexico Administrative Code § 20.6.4.7 S (5) defines surface water(s) of the state as:

        “(a) means all surface waters situated wholly or partly within or bordering upon the state,
        including the following:
               (i) lakes;
               (ii) rivers;
               (iii) streams (including intermittent and ephemeral streams);
               (iv) mudflats;
               (v) sandflats;
               (vi) wetlands;
               (vii) sloughs;
               (viii) prairie potholes;
               (ix) wet meadows;
               (x) playa lakes;
               (xi) reservoirs; and
               (xii) natural ponds.
        (b) also means all tributaries of such waters, including adjacent wetlands, any manmade
        bodies of water that were originally created in surface waters of the state or resulted in
        the impoundment of surface waters of the state, and any "waters of the United States"
        as defined under the Clean Water Act that are not included in the preceding description.
        (c) does not include private waters that do not combine with other surface or subsurface
        water or any water under tribal regulatory jurisdiction pursuant to Section 518 of the
        Clean Water Act. Waste treatment systems, including treatment ponds or lagoons
        designed and actively used to meet requirements of the Clean Water Act (other than
        cooling ponds as defined in 40 CFR Part 423.11(m) that also meet the criteria of this
        definition), are not surface waters of the state, unless they were originally created in
        surface waters of the state or resulted in the impoundment of surface waters of the
        state.”

                                                    4
                                                                                    EXP Energy Services, Inc.
                                                          DSW Aquatic Resource Inventory Report: New Mexico
                                                                                                   July 2026




Surveyors recorded these features as they were encountered.

Of particular relevance to the Project, New Mexico includes intermittent and ephemeral streams under
the definition of a surface water of the state. Consequently, ephemeral dry washes may be subject to
regulation in New Mexico. With regards to pipeline construction, the New Mexico Environment
Department (NMED) has certified Nationwide Permit (NWP) 12 with conditions. Nationwide Permit 12
applies to oil and natural gas pipeline activities. However, beginning in 2028 it is likely that New Mexico’s
state permitting program will begin issuing separate permits for work in waters of the state, including
potentially ephemeral dry washes (NMED 2026).

1.3 County Waters
No county in New Mexico crossed by the Project defines or regulates county waters.

1.4 Wetlands
Wetlands are defined in federal law per 33 C.F.R. § 328.3 (c)(1) as:

        “Wetlands means those areas that are inundated or saturated by surface or ground water
        at a frequency and duration sufficient to support, and that under normal circumstances
        do support, a prevalence of vegetation typically adapted for life in saturated soil
        conditions. Wetlands generally include swamps, marshes, bogs, and similar areas.”

New Mexico defines wetlands consistent with the federal definition (NMAC 20.6.4.7 W (4)).


2.0         Methods
2.1 Existing Data Review
Prior to field survey, potential wetlands, as well as non-wetland WOTUS (termed “waterbodies” in this
report), were identified in the Project area through publicly available data, including the National Wetland
Inventory (NWI) Data available through the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) (n.d.), the National
Hydrography Dataset (NHD) available through the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) (2026), and the Web Soil
Survey, Soil Survey Geographic (SSURGO) Database (Soil Survey Staff 2026).
Wetlands Climate Tables (WETS tables) developed by the NRCS were consulted prior to survey to confirm
that the delineation would take place within the growing season per U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE)
guidelines. March 16 is reported as the median growing season start (50 percent probability of being at
or above 28 degrees Fahrenheit) as averaged from two Agricultural Applied Climate Information System
(AgACIS) stations (State University Las Cruces, New Mexico (AgACIS 2026a), Deming Municipal Airport,



                                                   5
                                                                                   EXP Energy Services, Inc.
                                                         DSW Aquatic Resource Inventory Report: New Mexico
                                                                                                  July 2026



New Mexico (AgACIS 2026b)). Although survey was initiated prior to March 16, wetland indicators were
still identifiable at the time of survey.

2.2 Field Survey
Wetland delineation and waterbody field surveys were conducted between February 17, 2026, and April
14, 2026. Field delineation was completed by John Beaver, Pete Christensen, Lacey Gunther, Nate Lund,
Ashley Bramblett, Devin Mendez, and Dan Culwell. John Beaver was the lead delineator and has over 30
years’ experience delineating wetlands and recording waterbodies throughout the western United States.
Other lead delineators were Pete Christensen and Lacey Gunther who have 20 years of experience and 7
years’ experience respectively delineating wetlands and recording waterbodies throughout the western
United States. Mr. Beaver and Mr. Christensen have completed wetland delineation training courses and
advanced hydric soils training. Ms. Gunther, Mr. Lund, and Mr. Culwell have all completed wetland
delineation training courses. Ms. Bramblett and Mr. Mendez assisted with data collection and managed
spatial data.
Surveys were conducted within a 400-foot Environmental Study Area (ESA), which was nominally 80 feet
to one side of the Project centerline and 320 feet to the other side. The narrow side of the ESA typically
followed existing pipeline infrastructure. Additional areas that were subsequently added to the ESA were
likewise surveyed if they were not coincident with the previous ESA corridor, or if the additional areas
were large and the existing data from the surveyed ESA could not confidently be extended to include
them.

        Waters of the United States Identification
Of particular interest for most projects are tributaries to interstate commerce WOTUS that maintain
relatively permanent, standing, or continuously flowing water, and wetlands adjacent to these tributaries.
A key characteristic for identifying these tributaries is the presence of an ordinary high water mark
(OHWM) as defined in 33 C.F.R. § 328.3 (c)(4):

        “Ordinary high water mark means that line on the shore established by the fluctuations
        of water and indicated by physical characteristics such as clear, natural line impressed on
        the bank, shelving, changes in the character of soil, destruction of terrestrial vegetation,
        the presence of litter and debris, or other appropriate means that consider the
        characteristics of the surrounding areas.”

A primary reference for identifying the OHWM is the National Ordinary High Water Mark Field Delineation
Manual for Rivers and Streams (David et al. 2025). However, regional guides are also helpful depending
on where a Project occurs. Because this Project occurs within the Arid West, an important secondary
source for identifying OHWM was A Field Guide to the Identification of the Ordinary High Water Mark
(OHWM) in the Arid West Region of the Western United States: A Delineation Manual (Lichvar and
McColley 2008). Both references were used to identify waterbodies as distinct from swales or erosional
features (e.g., small washes, rills) that may occasionally convey water but that are not jurisdictional


                                                   6
                                                                                  EXP Energy Services, Inc.
                                                        DSW Aquatic Resource Inventory Report: New Mexico
                                                                                                 July 2026



WOTUS (33 C.F.R. § 328.3 (b)(8)), although they could be jurisdictional under New Mexico state law in
some situations.

In the Arid West, the most problematic OHWM delineations are associated with the commonly occurring
ephemeral/intermittent channel forms (e.g., dry washes) that dominate the Arid West landscape (Lichvar
and McColley 2008). In particular, the traditional use of OHWM indicators to identify the limits of non-
wetland waters is confounded in the Arid West by highly variable flow pathways within the channel
(Lichvar and McColley 2008).

Further, in the Arid West, the OHWM is often defined by the active floodplain: “The OHWM zone in low-
gradient, alluvial ephemeral/intermittent channel forms in the Arid West is the active floodplain. The
dynamics of arid channel forms and the transitory nature of traditional OHWM indicators in arid
environments render the limit of the active floodplain the only reliable and repeatable feature in terms
of OHW delineation” (Lichvar and McColley 2008).

If areas were identified as potential waterbodies based on NWI or NHD mapping, they were examined in
the field to determine if an OHWM was present as defined above. If an OHWM was not observed in areas
where they were indicated by NWI or NHD data, these areas were recorded as a non-feature. An “X” code
was used for features without evidence of any concentrated flow, an “E” code was used for features where
minimal rilling or flow was observed but where an OHWM was not present.

In addition to features identified in NWI or NHD mapping, the entire Project ESA was searched for
waterbodies that could be present but that are not mapped in either the NWI or NHD datasets.

Where an OHWM was encountered, it was mapped within the Project area using a Trimble R1 Global
Positioning System (GPS) antenna with submeter accuracy paired to ESRI Field Maps application and
classified according to hydrologic regime (perennial, intermittent, or ephemeral).

        Waters of the United States Hydrologic Regime
All features (channels, ponds, lakes, impoundments) with an OHWM were recorded during field surveys;
however, not all of those features are jurisdictional WOTUS, although they may be jurisdictional according
to some state regulations. In particular, determining whether a feature with an OHWM contains relatively
permanent water is a key determinant of its potential jurisdictional status. The USACE and Environmental
Protection Agency (EPA) define streamflow duration as follows:

     “Ephemeral reaches are channels that flow only in direct response to precipitation. Water
     typically flows only during and/or shortly after large precipitation events, the streambed is
     always above the water table, and stormwater runoff is the primary water source.

     Intermittent reaches are channels that contain sustained flowing water for only part of the year,
     typically during the wet season, where the streambed may be below the water table and/or


                                                  7
                                                                                   EXP Energy Services, Inc.
                                                         DSW Aquatic Resource Inventory Report: New Mexico
                                                                                                  July 2026



     where the snowmelt from surrounding uplands provides sustained flow. The flow may vary
     greatly with stormwater runoff.

     Perennial reaches are channels that contain flowing water continuously during a year of normal
     rainfall, often with the streambed located below the water table for most of the year.
     Groundwater typically supplies the baseflow for perennial reaches, but the baseflow may also
     be supplemented by stormwater runoff and/or snowmelt.” (Mazor et al., 2024)

Channels, coulees, gullies, or dry washes that are “ephemeral” and that only contain surface water flowing
or pooling in direct response to precipitation (e.g., rain or snow) were determined to be non-jurisdictional
features based on the U.S. Supreme Court’s Sackett v. Environmental Protection Agency ruling on May 25,
2023. These types of features are usually readily identifiable because they clearly lack evidence of
relatively permanent water such as: hydrophytic vegetation, ponded water or evidence of ponding, soil
cracking, aquatic invertebrates, or algal cover, and frequently have either rooted upland vegetation within
the channel or scoured bare soil in drier, erosive environments.

Similarly, perennial waters that flow or contain water continuously during a year of normal rainfall, are
usually readily identifiable because they contain water in dry periods, show continuous water presence
on aerial imagery, typically have hydrophytic vegetation within and/or immediately adjacent to the water,
and have evidence of aquatic invertebrates, algal cover, or other indicators of consistent water. Perennial
waters are often jurisdictional as they are relatively permanent waters that typically connect to, or are
themselves, interstate waters.

Ephemeral and perennial features are typically classified during field surveys without additional
investigation. However, many features with an OHWM have an apparent intermittent hydrologic regime
which requires further investigation to determine if the feature is a relatively permanent water. This
includes both features that do have an intermittent hydrologic regime, as well as ephemeral features that
may occasionally contain water at the time of survey due to recent precipitation, or perennial features
that occasionally do not contain water at the time of survey due to drought and/or upstream water
management. In these cases, a Stream Duration Assessment Method (SDAM) form (Mazor et al. 2024)
may be completed to determine the hydrologic regime; the SDAM data may be used by the USACE or
other appropriate agencies for assistance in determining jurisdiction. SDAM forms were completed during
survey at named washes, unnamed large washes, and named canals and ditches. SDAM forms were not
completed at smaller washes as it was readily apparent they met the definition of ephemeral flow.

        Wetland Delineation
Wetlands were delineated in accordance with the USACE Wetland Delineation Manual (Environmental
Laboratory 1987), the Regional Supplement to the Corps of Engineers Wetland Delineation Manual: Arid
West Region, Version 2.0 (USACE 2008) and the recently published Field Indicators of Hydric Soils in the
United States (USDA 2026).




                                                   8
                                                                                   EXP Energy Services, Inc.
                                                         DSW Aquatic Resource Inventory Report: New Mexico
                                                                                                  July 2026



The wetland delineation protocols consist of evaluating vegetation, soils, and hydrology at representative
plots within and adjacent to potential wetland areas. Unless a site has been significantly disturbed,
positive wetland indicators are normally recorded relative to vegetation, soils, and hydrology for a site to
meet the definition of a wetland as noted in the USACE Wetland Delineation Manual (Environmental
Laboratory 1987):

        “Except in certain situations defined in this manual, evidence of a minimum of one positive
        wetland indicator from each parameter (hydrology, soil, and vegetation) must be found in order
        to make a positive wetland determination.”

All areas mapped as a potential wetland with NWI data were evaluated. If the NWI wetland was clearly
not a wetland (e.g., dominated by Upland plants without any evidence of previous or current wetland
conditions), it was recorded as a non-feature with a point mapped in the field using a Trimble R1 GPS
antenna with submeter accuracy paired to ESRI Field Maps application. Photographs and habitat notes
were recorded at all non-features.

Where NWI-mapped wetlands appeared to contain a wetland, and at all areas where wetlands were
observed or suspected regardless of NWI mapping, sample plots were established. Paired plots were
established and located close to the wetland boundary to document the change from wetland to upland.

Sample plot locations were mapped in the field using a Trimble R1 GPS antenna with submeter accuracy
paired to ESRI Field Maps application.

Where wetlands were indicated or suspected, the following procedures were employed to
evaluate vegetation, soils, and hydrology relative to wetland delineation criteria.

2.2.3.1 Vegetation
The USACE wetland delineation methodology uses a plant community approach to determine whether a
site has hydrophytic vegetation, dominated by species that require or can tolerate prolonged inundation
or soil saturation during the growing season (Environmental Laboratory 1987). The USACE updates and
maintains the National Wetland Plant List (NWPL), in which vascular plant species are assigned a wetland
indicator status based on frequency of occurrence in wetlands (USACE 2023). The following wetland
indicator status ratings are used for the NWPL:


      Wetland Indicator Status        Definition1
      Obligate Wetland (OBL)          Almost always occur in wetlands
      Facultative Wetland (FACW)      Usually occur in wetlands, but may occur in non-wetlands
      Facultative (FAC)               Occur in wetlands or non-wetlands
      Facultative Upland (FACU)       Usually occur in non-wetlands, but may occur in wetlands
      Obligate Upland (UPL)           Almost never occur in wetlands
      1
        More complete definitions are given by Lichvar et al. (2012).

                                                   9
                                                                                     EXP Energy Services, Inc.
                                                           DSW Aquatic Resource Inventory Report: New Mexico
                                                                                                    July 2026



Presence of hydrophytic vegetation was noted based on one or more of the following tests (USACE, 2008):
        •   Rapid Test.
        •   Dominance Test.
        •   Prevalence Index.
A Rapid Test is considered a positive indicator if all dominant species across all strata are rated as obligate
or facultative wetland, or a combination of these two categories.
A Dominance Test is considered a positive indicator if 50 percent of the dominant plant species across all
strata are rated as obligate, facultative wetland, or facultative. Dominants are the most abundant species
that individually or collectively account for more than 50 percent of the total vegetative cover in the
stratum, plus other species that account for at least 20 percent of the total plant coverage.
The Prevalence Index is a weighted-average wetland indictor status for all plant species in the sampling
plot. Plants were grouped by indicator status and their individual coverages totaled. Each indicator status
group was given a numeric number: OBL – 1; FACW– 2; FAC – 3; FACU – 4; and UPL – 5. The numeric value
was multiplied by the summed vegetative coverages and these results were added together. The resulting
sum was divided by the total vegetative cover found on the sample plot to provide the final “Index.” Index
values of 3 or less indicate hydrophytic vegetation.

2.2.3.2 Soils
Hydric soils are defined as soils that are saturated, flooded, or ponded long enough during the growing
season to develop anaerobic conditions in the upper soil horizons (USDA 1991). Generally, hydric soils
are saturated, flooded, or ponded for one week or more during the period when soil temperatures are
above biologic zero (41 degrees Fahrenheit or 5 degrees Celsius), as defined in Soil Taxonomy Agriculture
Handbook #436 (Soil Survey Staff 1999). These soils typically support hydrophytic vegetation and exhibit
distinctive characteristics (e.g. redox features, depleted matrix, thick dark surface, etc.) that result from
repeated, extended periods of saturation; these characteristics tend to persist in the soil during both wet
and dry periods. A compilation of hydric soils indicators is included in Field Indicators of Hydric Soils in the
United States (USDA 2026). Region-specific indicators are discussed in the Regional Supplement (USACE
2008).
Shallow pits approximately 20 inches deep were dug at each wetland or upland plot to typify soils and
determine if hydric indicators were present. Soil horizons and characteristics were described, and any
hydric soil indicators present were recorded according to criteria noted in the Regional Supplement
(USACE 2008) and Field Indicators of Hydric Soils in the United States (USDA 2026).

2.2.3.3 Hydrology
The presence of wetland hydrology is inferred from hydrologic indicators of repeated, extended episodes
of inundation or soil saturation (e.g., surface water, saturation, oxidized rhizospheres along living roots,
drainage patterns, geomorphic position, and frost-heave hummocks) (USACE 2008). Field investigations
included walking all areas, with survey permission, that were determined to potentially support wetlands


                                                    10
                                                                                   EXP Energy Services, Inc.
                                                         DSW Aquatic Resource Inventory Report: New Mexico
                                                                                                  July 2026



and noting the presence and extent of hydrologic indicators. Shallow pits (approximately 20 inches deep)
were excavated for hydric soil investigations at wetland plots and adjacent upland sites. These same soil
pits were also used to determine presence and depth to a shallow water table, depth to soil saturation,
oxidized rhizospheres along living roots, or other hydrologic indicators.

2.2.3.4 Integration of Wetland Components
Generally, indicators of all three wetland components must be present for an area to be considered a
wetland. The 1987 USACE manual states:
        “Except in certain situations defined in this manual, evidence of a minimum of one
        positive wetland indicator from each parameter (hydrology, soil, and vegetation) must be
        found in order to make a positive wetland determination.”
Based on data collected for vegetation, soils, and hydrology, delineators identified vegetation,
topographic, and/or hydrologic features that were indicative of areas where all three wetland criteria
were met. Once consistent features of the boundary between wetlands and uplands were discerned, the
boundary between each wetland and the adjacent upland was walked and the boundary recorded using
a sub-meter Trimble R1 GPS antenna paired to ESRI Field Maps application.

        Wetland Jurisdiction
Although a site may meet the definition of a wetland aper the USACE Wetland Delineation Manual
(Environmental Laboratory 1987), the wetland may not be jurisdictional at the federal level if there is not
a continuous surface connection between it and a jurisdictional WOTUS. After the Sackett v.
Environmental Protection Agency decision, the USACE and EPA issued joint guidance to identify a
continuous surface connection between a wetland and a jurisdictional water (USACE and EPA 2025a,
2025b). This guidance clarifies that:
        “First, the adjacent body of water must be a “water of the United States,” which generally
        means traditional navigable waters, or a relatively permanent body of water connected
        to a traditional navigable water. Second, the wetland, assuming it satisfies the agencies’
        longstanding regulatory definition of “wetlands” at 33 C.F.R. 328.3 and 40 C.F.R. 120.2,
        must have a continuous surface connection to a requisite covered water making it difficult
        to determine where the water ends and wetland begins.”
Based on that guidance, delineators investigated each wetland to determine if a continuous surface
connection existed between the wetland and WOTUS.

3.1 Waterbodies
The NWI dataset identified 148 riverine waterbody crossings within the Project ESA in New Mexico, all of
which are coded R4SB indicating that they are either intermittent or ephemeral riverine features. The
NWI dataset also identified seven, small, constructed impoundments within the ESA and one lake –
Lordsburg Playa.

WESTECH identified a total of 144 waterbody crossings using the methods described Sections 2.2.1 and
2.2.2, and an additional 22 crossings via desktop for areas that were not available for survey or where
minor changes to the ESA resulted in new features being included adjacent to previously surveyed areas.
The term waterbody is somewhat misleading for these linear features; all contained an OHWM but none
were flowing at the time of survey. The vast majority of features are dry washes. Delineators also
recorded 145 rills or other erosional features that showed evidence of occasional water movement but
that did not contain an OHWM as water is so minimally present that it does not develop a distinct bed
and bank.

The only river recorded in New Mexico within the ESA is the Rio Grande near Las Cruces, New Mexico. No
water was present in the river during the entire period of survey when delineators were either at the ESA
crossing or working in the vicinity of the Rio Grande.
The majority of features within the ESA are dry washes which flow in direct response to precipitation and
form an OHWM. None of these features contained water at the time of survey. A few features were
described as gullies, indicating that they were steep and substantially deeper than wide; however, like the
dry washes, water was not present in any gully at the time of survey.
The largest feature within the Project ESA in New Mexico is the Lordsburg Playa. The playa was mostly
dry at the time of survey, although some small puddles and sheets of water were noted near the ESA and
particularly adjacent to Interstate 10 about 2.5 miles south of the ESA. Delineators completed wetland
delineation forms near the playa OHWM to determine if hydric soils were present; none were (Appendix
A). In this case, the OHWM appeared as the area that corresponded to a slight change in vegetation (more
vegetation is present outside the playa) and slight evidence of a slope change. Delineators also excavated
soil pits approximately every 0.5-mile within the playa to assess soils. None of these investigations found
hydric soil indicators. Soil colors in the Lordsburg Playa were 7.5Y 5/3, 7.5Y 5/4, and 7.5Y 6/3. Soil color
above the OHWM was 7.5Y 6/3. None of these colors indicate hydric conditions and other indicators,
such as redox features, were not observed. Most of the Lordsburg Playa is unvegetated with sporadic
plants of fourwing saltbush (Atriplex canescens), alkali sacaton (Sporobolus arioides), and shadscale
saltbush (Atriplex confertifolia); both saltbushes are upland species and alkali sacaton is FAC. Hydrophytic
vegetation is not present within the playa, nor are hydric soils; consequently, although the playa clearly
holds water at different times of the year, it is not a wetland but rather a waterbody.

        Waterbody Hydrology
SDAM forms were completed 17 features in New Mexico, including the Rio Grande River, named washes,
larger unnamed washes, and named canals and ditches (Appendix B). None of these features contained
indicators of perennial hydrology, and only one feature, the Rio Grande River was classified as
intermittent. However, this classification was based on the NWI classification for the river rather than
conditions within the ESA; those conditions appeared more consistent with ephemeral flow in direct
response to precipitation. All other natural features (i.e., dry washes and gullies) were classified as
ephemeral hydrology while constructed canals and ditches were classified as artificial hydrology, meaning
flow is artificial and a result of flooding controlled by pumps, siphons, dikes, or dams (Cowardin et al.,
1979).

3.2 Wetlands
The NWI dataset identified three wetlands within the Project ESA. WESTECH delineated one wetland
within the Project ESA using the methods described in Section 2.2.3. The wetland is within an
impoundment in Doña Ana County east of Las Cruces and is dominated by rough cocklebur (Xanthium
strumarium). The other NWI wetlands were investigated and found to lack hydric soil and hydrophytic
vegetation although all were within old, excavated impoundments.

3.3 Waters of the United States
Waterbody and wetland jurisdictional status is defined in Section 2.2.4. Jurisdictional determinations are
made by the USACE, EPA, and state agencies with regulatory oversight. Appendix C presents a line list of
linear features with an OHWM, features that may hold open water, and the wetland within the Project
ESA in New Mexico to facilitate that determination. None of the waterbody-type features within the
Project ESA are currently used, or were used in the past, or may be susceptible to use in interstate or
foreign commerce. Further, none of the waterbodies exhibit more than intermittent flow, indicating that
most features are not relatively permanent waters. Similarly, the single wetland within the Project ESA is
a constructed impoundment on an ephemeral wash. Consequently, it appears that none of the features
recorded during field delineations meet the definition of a WOTUS.

        Waters of the State: New Mexico
As described in Section 1.2, New Mexico includes intermittent and ephemeral streams under the
definition of a surface water of the state. Consequently, ephemeral dry washes may be subject to
regulation in New Mexico. Beginning in 2028 it is likely that New Mexico’s state permitting program will
begin issuing separate permits for work in waters of the state, including potentially ephemeral dry washes
(NMED 2026).

1.0         Introduction
Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC (Transwestern), a wholly-owned subsidiary of Energy Transfer LP
(Energy Transfer), is seeking authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or
Commission) pursuant to Section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act (NGA) to construct, own, and operate the
proposed Desert Southwest Expansion Project (DSWE Project or Project). The Project is an expansion of
the existing Transwestern system that will consist of approximately 525.2 miles of 48-inch diameter
mainline pipeline (mainline) and approximately 180.0 miles associated with 13 lateral pipelines (laterals),
as well as new compressor stations, associated meter stations, and other aboveground facilities located
in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. The Project will provide firm transportation service of up to 2.3 billion
cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) of natural gas from the Permian Basin to delivery points serving customers in
New Mexico and Arizona and will upgrade Transwestern’s existing Phoenix Lateral to allow bi-directional
flow.
The Project location in Arizona is portrayed in Figure 1.
WESTECH Environmental Services, Inc. (WESTECH) was contracted to Transwestern to survey and
delineate aquatic resources along the Project that may require permitting and/or particular construction
and mitigation measures. This report documents desktop analysis and field surveys that were completed
to identify, delineate, and map aquatic resources along the proposed Project route in Arizona.

1.1 Definitions
The following sections define the types of features that were surveyed in this report.

        Waters of the United States
Waters of the United States (WOTUS) are defined in 33 C.F.R. § 328.3 (a) as the following:

        (a) Waters of the United States means:
         (1) Waters which are:
             (i) Currently used, or were used in the past, or may be susceptible to use in interstate
             or foreign commerce, including all waters which are subject to the ebb and flow of
             the tide;
             (ii) The territorial seas; or
             (iii) Interstate waters;
        (2) Impoundments of waters otherwise defined as waters of the United States under this
        definition, other than impoundments of waters identified under paragraph (a)(5) of this
        section;
        (3) Tributaries of waters identified in paragraph (a)(1) or (2) of this section that are
        relatively permanent, standing or continuously flowing bodies of water;
        (4) Wetlands adjacent to the following waters:

             (i) Waters identified in paragraph (a)(1) of this section; or(ii) Relatively permanent,
             standing or continuously flowing bodies of water identified in paragraph (a)(2) or
             (a)(3) of this section and with a continuous surface connection to those waters;
        (5) Intrastate lakes and ponds not identified in paragraphs (a)(1) through (4) of this section
        that are relatively permanent, standing or continuously flowing bodies of water with a
        continuous surface connection to the waters identified in paragraph (a)(1) or (a)(3) of this
        section.

1.2 Waters of the State: Arizona
The state of Arizona has a somewhat more expansive definition of waters of the state compared to the
definition of WOTUS. Arizona Revised Statues 49-201.50 defines waters of the state as:

        "Waters of the state means all waters within the jurisdiction of this state including all
        perennial or intermittent streams, lakes, ponds, impounding reservoirs, marshes,
        watercourses, waterways, wells, aquifers, springs, irrigation systems, drainage systems
        and other bodies or accumulations of surface, underground, natural, artificial, public or
        private water situated wholly or partly in or bordering on the state.”

Surveyors recorded these features as they were encountered.

1.3 County Waters
Both Pima and Pinal counties have regulations or guidelines regarding riparian areas within each county;
these riparian areas typically surround dry washes, streams, and excavated impoundments. In Pima
County, ordinance 16.30 identifies watercourse and riparian habitat protection and mitigation measures.
Pima County has mapped “regulated riparian habitat” according to four categories: hydroriparian,
mesoriparian, xeroriparian, and important riparian habitats (Pima County 2026a); these areas identify
locations where a Floodplain Use Permit may be required prior to vegetation clearing.

Pinal County has issued non-regulatory guidelines to “identify, protect, and reduce impacts to riparian
areas throughout the County” (Pinal County 2019).

Riparian mapping in Pima and Pinal counties was downloaded to review these features during
field surveys.

1.4 Wetlands
Wetlands are defined in federal law per 33 C.F.R. § 328.3 (c)(1) as:

        “Wetlands means those areas that are inundated or saturated by surface or ground water
        at a frequency and duration sufficient to support, and that under normal circumstances
                                                    3
                                                                                   EXP Energy Services, Inc.
                                                              DSW Aquatic Resource Inventory Report: Arizona
                                                                                                  July 2026



        do support, a prevalence of vegetation typically adapted for life in saturated soil
        conditions. Wetlands generally include swamps, marshes, bogs, and similar areas.”

Arizona defines wetlands consistent with the federal definition (AZAC R-18-11-101 (53)).


2.0         Methods
2.1 Existing Data Review
Prior to field survey, potential wetlands, as well as non-wetland WOTUS (termed “waterbodies” in this
report), were identified in the Project area through publicly available data, including the National Wetland
Inventory (NWI) Data available through the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) (n.d.), the National
Hydrography Dataset (NHD) available through the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) (2026), and the Web Soil
Survey, Soil Survey Geographic (SSURGO) Database (Soil Survey Staff 2026). Finally, spatial data from both
Pima and Pinal counties were downloaded so that county-mapped riparian areas could be mapped and
assessed during field surveys (Pima County 2026b, AGFD 2024).
Wetlands Climate Tables (WETS tables) developed by the NRCS were consulted prior to survey to confirm
that the delineation would take place within the growing season per U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE)
guidelines. March 3 is reported as the median growing season start (50 percent probability of being at or
above 28 degrees Fahrenheit) as averaged from three Agricultural Applied Climate Information System
(AgACIS) stations Wilcox, Arizona (AgACIS 2026a), San Manuel, Arizona (AgACIS 2026b), and Gila Bend 2SE
(AgACIS 2026c)). However, the growing season typically begins around April 2 in Wilcox whereas it
typically begins around January 28 in San Manuel and Gila Bend. Field surveys were initiated slightly
before March 3 but a wetland was not encountered until March 4.

2.2 Field Survey
Wetland delineation and waterbody field surveys were conducted between February 25, 2026, and June
12, 2026. Field delineation was completed by John Beaver, Pete Christensen, Lacey Gunther, Nate Lund,
Ashley Bramblett, Devin Mendez, and Dan Culwell. John Beaver was the lead delineator and has over 30
years’ experience delineating wetlands and recording waterbodies throughout the western United States.
Other lead delineators were Pete Christensen and Lacey Gunther who have 20 years of experience and 7
years’ experience respectively delineating wetlands and recording waterbodies throughout the western
United States. Mr. Beaver and Mr. Christensen have completed wetland delineation training courses and
advanced hydric soils training. Ms. Gunther, Mr. Lund, and Mr. Culwell have all completed wetland
delineation training courses. Ms. Bramblett and Mr. Mendez assisted with data collection and managed
spatial data.
Surveys were conducted within a 400-foot Environmental Study Area (ESA), which was nominally 80 feet
to one side of the Project centerline and 320 feet to the other side. The narrow side of the ESA typically
followed existing pipeline infrastructure. Additional areas that were subsequently added to the ESA were

                                                   4
                                                                                     EXP Energy Services, Inc.
                                                                DSW Aquatic Resource Inventory Report: Arizona
                                                                                                    July 2026



likewise surveyed if they were not coincident with the previous ESA corridor, or if the additional areas
were large and the existing data from the surveyed ESA could not confidently be extended to include
them.

        Waters of the United States Identification
Of particular interest for most projects are tributaries to interstate commerce WOTUS that maintain
relatively permanent, standing, or continuously flowing water, and wetlands adjacent to these tributaries.
A key characteristic for identifying these tributaries is the presence of an ordinary high water mark
(OHWM) as defined in 33 C.F.R. § 328.3 (c)(4):
        “Ordinary high water mark means that line on the shore established by the fluctuations
        of water and indicated by physical characteristics such as clear, natural line impressed on
        the bank, shelving, changes in the character of soil, destruction of terrestrial vegetation,
        the presence of litter and debris, or other appropriate means that consider the
        characteristics of the surrounding areas.”
A primary reference for identifying the OHWM is the National Ordinary High Water Mark Field Delineation
Manual for Rivers and Streams (David et al. 2025). However, regional guides are also helpful depending
on where a Project occurs. Because the Project occurs within the Arid West, an important secondary
source for identifying OHWM was A Field Guide to the Identification of the Ordinary High Water Mark
(OHWM) in the Arid West Region of the Western United States: A Delineation Manual (Lichvar and
McColley 2008). Both references were used to identify waterbodies as distinct from swales or erosional
features (e.g., gullies, small washes, rills) that may occasionally convey water but that are not jurisdictional
WOTUS (33 C.F.R. § 328.3 (b)(8)), although they could be jurisdictional under Arizona state law in some
situations.
In the Arid West, the most problematic OHWM delineations are associated with the commonly occurring
ephemeral/intermittent channel forms that dominate the Arid West landscape (Lichvar and McColley
2008). In particular, the traditional use of OHWM indicators to identify the limits of non-wetland waters
is confounded in the Arid West by highly variable flow pathways within the channel (Lichvar and McColley
2008).
Further, in the Arid West, the OHWM is often defined by the active floodplain: “The OHWM zone in low-
gradient, alluvial ephemeral/intermittent channel forms in the Arid West is the active floodplain. The
dynamics of arid channel forms and the transitory nature of traditional OHWM indicators in arid
environments render the limit of the active floodplain the only reliable and repeatable feature in terms
of OHW delineation” (Lichvar and McColley 2008).
If areas were identified as potential waterbodies based on NWI or NHD mapping, they were examined in
the field to determine if an OHWM was present as defined above. If an OHWM was not observed in areas
where they were indicated by NWI or NHD data, these areas were recorded as a non-feature. An “X” code
was used for features without evidence of any concentrated flow, an “E” code was used for features where
minimal rilling or flow was observed but where an OHWM was not present.

In addition to features identified in NWI or NHD mapping, the entire Project ESA was searched for
waterbodies that could be present but that are not mapped in either the NWI or NHD datasets.
Where an OHWM was encountered, it was mapped within the Project area using a Trimble R1 GPS
antenna with submeter accuracy paired to ESRI Field Maps application and classified according to
hydrologic regime (perennial, intermittent, or ephemeral).

        Waters of the United States Hydrologic Regime
All features (channels, ponds, lakes, impoundments) with an OHWM were recorded during field surveys;
however, not all of those features are jurisdictional WOTUS, although they may be jurisdictional according
to some state regulations. In particular, determining whether a feature with an OHWM contains relatively
permanent water is a key determinant of its potential jurisdictional status. The USACE and Environmental
Protection Agency (EPA) define streamflow duration as follows:
        “Ephemeral reaches are channels that flow only in direct response to precipitation. Water
        typically flows only during and/or shortly after large precipitation events, the streambed
        is always above the water table, and stormwater runoff is the primary water source.
        Intermittent reaches are channels that contain sustained flowing water for only part of
        the year, typically during the wet season, where the streambed may be below the water
        table and/or where the snowmelt from surrounding uplands provides sustained flow. The
        flow may vary greatly with stormwater runoff.
        Perennial reaches are channels that contain flowing water continuously during a year of
        normal
        rainfall, often with the streambed located below the water table for most of the year.
        Groundwater typically supplies the baseflow for perennial reaches, but the baseflow may
        also be supplemented by stormwater runoff and/or snowmelt.” (Mazor et al., 2024)
Channels, coulees, gullies, or dry washes that are “ephemeral” and that only contain surface water flowing
or pooling in direct response to precipitation (e.g., rain or snow) were determined to be non-jurisdictional
features based on the U.S. Supreme Court’s Sackett v. Environmental Protection Agency ruling on May 25,
2023. These types of features are usually readily identifiable because they clearly lack evidence of
relatively permanent water such as: hydrophytic vegetation, ponded water or evidence of ponding, soil
cracking, aquatic invertebrates, or algal cover, and frequently have either rooted upland vegetation within
the channel or scoured bare soil in drier, erosive environments.
Similarly, perennial waters that flow or contain water continuously during a year of normal rainfall, are
usually readily identifiable because they contain water in dry periods, show continuous water presence
on aerial imagery, typically have hydrophytic vegetation within and/or immediately adjacent to the water,
and have evidence of aquatic invertebrates, algal cover, or other indicators of consistent water. Perennial
waters are often jurisdictional as they are relatively permanent waters that typically connect to, or are
themselves, interstate waters.

                                                                                   EXP Energy Services, Inc.
                                                              DSW Aquatic Resource Inventory Report: Arizona
                                                                                                  July 2026



Ephemeral and perennial features are typically classified during field surveys without additional
investigation. However, many features with an OHWM have an apparent intermittent hydrologic regime
which requires further investigation to determine if the feature is a relatively permanent water. This
includes both features that do have an intermittent hydrologic regime, as well as ephemeral features that
may occasionally contain water at the time of survey due to recent precipitation, or perennial features
that occasionally do not contain water at the time of survey due to drought and/or upstream water
management. In these cases, a Stream Duration Assessment Method (SDAM) form (Mazor et al. 2024)
may be completed to determine the hydrologic regime; the SDAM data may be used by the USACE or
other appropriate agencies for assistance in determining jurisdiction. SDAM forms were completed during
survey at named washes, unnamed large washes, and named canals and ditches. SDAM forms were not
completed at smaller washes as it was readily apparent they met the definition of ephemeral flow.

        Wetland Delineation
Wetlands were delineated in accordance with the USACE Wetland Delineation Manual (Environmental
Laboratory 1987), the Regional Supplement to the Corps of Engineers Wetland Delineation Manual: Arid
West Region, Version 2.0 (USACE 2008) and the recently published Field Indicators of Hydric Soils in the
United States (USDA 2026).

The wetland delineation protocols consist of evaluating vegetation, soils, and hydrology at representative
plots within and adjacent to potential wetland areas. Unless a site has been significantly disturbed,
positive wetland indicators are normally recorded relative to vegetation, soils, and hydrology for a site to
meet the definition of a wetland as noted in the USACE Wetland Delineation Manual (Environmental
Laboratory 1987):

        “Except in certain situations defined in this manual, evidence of a minimum of one positive
        wetland indicator from each parameter (hydrology, soil, and vegetation) must be found in order
        to make a positive wetland determination.”

All areas mapped as a potential wetland with NWI data were evaluated. If the NWI wetland was clearly
not a wetland (e.g., dominated by Upland plants without any evidence of previous or current wetland
conditions), it was recorded as a non-feature with a point mapped in the field using a Trimble R1 GPS
antenna with submeter accuracy paired to ESRI Field Maps application. Photographs and habitat notes
were recorded at all non-features.

Where NWI-mapped wetlands appeared to contain a wetland, and at all areas where wetlands were
observed or suspected regardless of NWI mapping, sample plots were established. Paired plots were
established and located close to the wetland boundary to document the change from wetland to upland.

Sample plot locations were mapped in the field using a Trimble R1 GPS antenna with submeter accuracy
paired to ESRI Field Maps application.

                                                                                    EXP Energy Services, Inc.
                                                               DSW Aquatic Resource Inventory Report: Arizona
                                                                                                   July 2026



Where wetlands were indicated or suspected, the following procedures were employed to
evaluate vegetation, soils, and hydrology relative to wetland delineation criteria.

2.2.3.1 Vegetation
The USACE wetland delineation methodology uses a plant community approach to determine whether a
site has hydrophytic vegetation, dominated by species that require or can tolerate prolonged inundation
or soil saturation during the growing season (Environmental Laboratory 1987). The USACE updates and
maintains the National Wetland Plant List (NWPL), in which vascular plant species are assigned a wetland
indicator status based on frequency of occurrence in wetlands (USACE 2023). The following wetland
indicator status ratings are used for the NWPL:


       Wetland Indicator Status        Definition1
       Obligate Wetland (OBL)          Almost always occur in wetlands
       Facultative Wetland (FACW)      Usually occur in wetlands, but may occur in non-wetlands
       Facultative (FAC)               Occur in wetlands or non-wetlands
       Facultative Upland (FACU)       Usually occur in non-wetlands, but may occur in wetlands
       Obligate Upland (UPL)           Almost never occur in wetlands
       1
         More complete definitions are given by Lichvar et al. (2012).
Presence of hydrophytic vegetation was noted based on one or more of the following tests (USACE, 2008):
        •   Rapid Test.
        •   Dominance Test.
        •   Prevalence Index.
A Rapid Test is considered a positive indicator if all dominant species across all strata are rated as obligate
or facultative wetland, or a combination of these two categories.
A Dominance Test is considered a positive indicator if 50 percent of the dominant plant species across all
strata are rated as obligate, facultative wetland, or facultative. Dominants are the most abundant species
that individually or collectively account for more than 50 percent of the total vegetative cover in the
stratum, plus other species that account for at least 20 percent of the total plant coverage.
The Prevalence Index is a weighted-average wetland indictor status for all plant species in the sampling
plot. Plants were grouped by indicator status and their individual coverages totaled. Each indicator status
group was given a numeric number: OBL – 1; FACW– 2; FAC – 3; FACU – 4; and UPL – 5. The numeric value
was multiplied by the summed vegetative coverages and these results were added together. The resulting
sum was divided by the total vegetative cover found on the sample plot to provide the final “Index.” Index
values of 3 or less indicate hydrophytic vegetation.

2.2.3.2 Soils
Hydric soils are defined as soils that are saturated, flooded, or ponded long enough during the growing
season to develop anaerobic conditions in the upper soil horizons (USDA 1991). Generally, hydric soils
are saturated, flooded, or ponded for one week or more during the period when soil temperatures are
                                                    8
                                                                                     EXP Energy Services, Inc.
                                                                DSW Aquatic Resource Inventory Report: Arizona
                                                                                                    July 2026



above biologic zero (41 degrees Fahrenheit or 5 degrees Celsius), as defined in Soil Taxonomy Agriculture
Handbook #436 (Soil Survey Staff 1999). These soils typically support hydrophytic vegetation and exhibit
distinctive characteristics (e.g. redox features, depleted matrix, thick dark surface, etc.) that result from
repeated, extended periods of saturation; these characteristics tend to persist in the soil during both wet
and dry periods. A compilation of hydric soils indicators is included in Field Indicators of Hydric Soils in the
United States (USDA 2026). Region-specific indicators are discussed in the Regional Supplement (USACE
2008).
Shallow pits approximately 20 inches deep were dug at each wetland or upland plot to typify soils and
determine if hydric indicators were present. Soil horizons and characteristics were described, and any
hydric soil indicators present were recorded according to criteria noted in the Regional Supplement
(USACE 2008) and Field Indicators of Hydric Soils in the United States (USDA 2026).

2.2.3.3 Hydrology
The presence of wetland hydrology is inferred from hydrologic indicators of repeated, extended episodes
of inundation or soil saturation (e.g., surface water, saturation, oxidized rhizospheres along living roots,
drainage patterns, geomorphic position, and frost-heave hummocks) (USACE 2008). Field investigations
included walking all areas, with survey permission, that were determined to potentially support wetlands
and noting the presence and extent of hydrologic indicators. Shallow pits (approximately 20 inches deep)
were excavated for hydric soil investigations at wetland plots and adjacent upland sites. These same soil
pits were also used to determine presence and depth to a shallow water table, depth to soil saturation,
oxidized rhizospheres along living roots, or other hydrologic indicators.

2.2.3.4 Integration of Wetland Components
Generally, indicators of all three wetland components must be present for an area to be considered a
wetland. The 1987 USACE manual states:
        “Except in certain situations defined in this manual, evidence of a minimum of one
        positive wetland indicator from each parameter (hydrology, soil, and vegetation) must be
        found in order to make a positive wetland determination.”
Based on data collected for vegetation, soils, and hydrology, delineators identified vegetation,
topographic, and/or hydrologic features that were indicative of areas where all three wetland criteria
were met. Once consistent features of the boundary between wetlands and uplands were discerned, the
boundary between each wetland and the adjacent upland was walked and the boundary recorded using
a sub-meter Trimble R1 GPS antenna paired to ESRI Field Maps application.

        Wetland Jurisdiction
Although a site may meet the definition of a wetland aper the USACE Wetland Delineation Manual
(Environmental Laboratory 1987), the wetland may not be jurisdictional at the federal level if there is not
a continuous surface connection between it and a jurisdictional WOTUS. After the Sackett v.
Environmental Protection Agency decision, the USACE and EPA issued joint guidance to identify a
                                                     9
                                                                                  EXP Energy Services, Inc.
                                                             DSW Aquatic Resource Inventory Report: Arizona
                                                                                                 July 2026



continuous surface connection between a wetland and a jurisdictional water (USACE and EPA 2025a,
2025b). This guidance clarifies that:
        “First, the adjacent body of water must be a “water of the United States,” which generally
        means traditional navigable waters, or a relatively permanent body of water connected
        to a traditional navigable water. Second, the wetland, assuming it satisfies the agencies’
        longstanding regulatory definition of “wetlands” at 33 C.F.R. 328.3 and 40 C.F.R. 120.2,
        must have a continuous surface connection to a requisite covered water making it difficult
        to determine where the water ends and wetland begins.”
Based on that guidance, delineators investigated each wetland to determine if a continuous surface
connection existed between the wetland and WOTUS.


3.0         Results
Appendix A presents wetland determination forms completed within the ESA in Arizona. SDAM forms are
provided in Appendix B with accompanying photos and insert maps of each feature. Appendix C presents
a line list of features with an OHWM, features that may hold open water, and the wetland identified within
the Project ESA in Arizona. Maps of all surveyed features are depicted in Appendix D. Spatial data are
provided separately.

3.1 Waterbodies
The NWI dataset identified 307 riverine waterbody crossings within the Project ESA in Arizona, all of which
are coded R4 or R5 indicating that they are either intermittent or ephemeral riverine features or have an
unknown hydrologic regime except for the following: San Pedro River, Bass Canyon, Gila River, Pima
Lateral Canal, Florence Casa Grande Canal, three crossings of the Central Arizona Project (CAP) Canal, and
one unnamed ditch in Maricopa County. All of these features are classified as R2UB in the NWI dataset
meaning they are lower perennial waterbodies (Cowardin et al. 1979).

The NWI dataset also identified 15 small, constructed impoundments within the ESA.

WESTECH identified a total of 675 waterbody crossings using the methods described Sections 2.2.1 and
2.2.2, and an additional 115 crossings via desktop for areas that were not available for survey or where
minor changes to the ESA resulted in new features being included adjacent to previously surveyed areas.
The term waterbody is somewhat misleading for these linear features; all contained an OHWM but only
Bass Canyon, Wildcat Canyon, Wood Canyon Wash, and the constructed canals were flowing at the time
of survey. The vast majority of features are dry washes. Delineators also recorded 362 rills or other
erosional features that showed evidence of occasional water movement but that did not contain an
OHWM as water is so minimally present that it does not develop a distinct bed and bank.

        Waterbody Hydrology
SDAM forms were completed 45 features in Arizona, including the Gila River, San Pedro River, Bass
Canyon, Wildcat Canyon, Wood Canyon Wash, other named washes, larger unnamed washes, and named
canals and ditches (Appendix B). The only features that might be perennial are two constructed ponds,
OW-WT3-CC-001 and OW-WT5-PN-001. These two ponds contained water at the time of survey and seem
to contain water most of the time based on aerial imagery and the assumption that the well sources that
artificially supply water to the ponds operate year-round. The large canals such as CAP, Florence, and Gila
Bend frequently contain water but are dry during periods of maintenance or during drought. The flow
regime at constructed canals and ditches was classified as artificial hydrology, meaning flow is artificial
and a result of flooding controlled by pumps, siphons, dikes, or dams (Cowardin et al., 1979).
The Project ESA intersects two rivers in Arizona, the San Pedro and the Gila. Both of these rivers are
categorized as lower perennial in the NWI dataset; however, neither were flowing at the time of survey
and both appeared to only flow in direct response to precipitation. Data from the SDAM assessment
indicates that both are ephemeral in the reach that includes the ESA.
Three natural features did contain flowing water at the time of survey: Bass Canyon, Wildcat Canyon, and
Wood Canyon Wash.
Bass Canyon is categorized as lower perennial in the NWI dataset and water was flowing at the time of
survey in March 2026. However, subsequent visits by other Project members found Bass Canyon to be
dry on June 15, 2026. These data are recorded on the SDAM form for Bass Canyon (Appendix B).
Intermittent flow in these drainages is apparently typical. A watershed improvement report found that
some portions of both Bass Canyon and the adjacent Hot Springs Canyon are perennial, while other
portions are intermittent (Brunson et al. 2001). This report includes hydrographic data from 1997 to 2000
near the Project ESA crossing of Bass Canyon and documented a lack of water from May until June or July
(Brunson et al. 2001).
Habitat was assessed in both areas in March 2026. In Bass Canyon, water was flowing within the stream
and was approximately 12 feet wide and approximately two to six inches deep. Some riparian vegetation
was in leaf and readily identifiable; however, several species were likely present that were not identifiable
at that time. The Project ESA at Bass Canyon is dominated by Fremont cottonwood (Populus fremontii)
and Arizona sycamore (Platanus wrightii) with an understory of Goodding’s willow (Salix gooddingii) and
scattered redberry juniper (Juniperus arizonica). Sedges (Carex sp.) also occur at the crossing but the
inflorescences were not well-developed in March, and the species could not be definitively identified,
although Cochise sedge (Carex ultra) is a possibility. Some scattered non-riparian plants are present on
gravel bars such as small melilot (Melilotus indicus). Surrounding upland slopes are dominated by the
Chihuahuan Mixed Desert and Thornscrub type.
Immediately northwest of Bass Canyon is Wildcat Canyon which has similar habitat to Bass Canyon, and
which was also flowing at the time of survey in March 2026. However, subsequent visits found Wildcat
Canyon to be dry on June 15, 2026. Consequently, both Bass Canyon and Wildcat Canyon were classified
as intermittent within the reach that includes the Project ESA.

The other natural feature with flowing water at the time of survey was Wood Canyon Wash in the
Winchester Mountains. Water was flowing in a very limited portion of the wash crossed by the ESA;
consequently, Wood Canyon Wash was classified as intermittent.
Other than these three natural features, two ponds, and the constructed canals, the majority of features
within the ESA are dry washes which flow in direct response to precipitation and form an OHWM. None
of these features contained water at the time of survey. A few features were described as gullies,
indicating that they were steep and substantially deeper than wide; however, like the dry washes, water
was not present in any gully at the time of survey. All of these natural features (i.e., dry washes and
gullies) were classified as having ephemeral hydrology.

3.2 Wetlands
The NWI dataset identified 20 wetlands within the Project ESA in Arizona. WESTECH delineated one
wetland using the methods described in Section 2.2.3. This wetland is located around the margins of the
potentially perennial pond, OW-WT3-CC-001, in Cochise County about 3 miles northwest of San Simon,
Arizona. Water is provided through a pipe from an adjacent windmill. The wetland is a narrow fringe that
surrounds the small pond and is dominated by alkali sacaton (Sporobolus airoides); soils are hydric. The
wetland and upland determination forms are presented in Appendix A.

The remaining NWI-identified wetlands are all mapped as forested/shrub wetlands but most were found
to either be ruderal (i.e., “weedy”) riparian vegetation dominated primarily by saltcedar (Tamarix spp.) or
mesquite (Neltuma spp.). Most of these sites are associated with Centennial Wash in Maricopa County
on the Harquahala Lateral. Centennial Wash is a mapped, but barely discernible feature throughout most
of the ESA. Wetlands were not observed along it. The other sites are a series of NWI features immediately
east of the CAP Canal near Randolph, Arizona in Pinal County. It is unclear why these areas were mapped
by NWI as wetlands; all these sites are uplands dominated by desert scrub species.

3.3 Waters of the United States
Waterbody and wetland jurisdictional status is defined in Section 2.2.4. Jurisdictional determinations are
made by the USACE, EPA, and state agencies with regulatory oversight. Appendix C presents a line list of
linear features with an OHWM, features that may hold open water, and the wetland within the Project
ESA in Arizona to facilitate that determination. None of the waterbody-type features within the Project
ESA are currently used, or were used in the past, or may be susceptible to use in interstate or foreign
commerce. Further, none of the waterbodies exhibit more than intermittent flow, with the possible
exception of two constructed ponds and constructed canals, indicating that most features are not
relatively permanent waters. Similarly, the single wetland within the Project ESA is a constructed
impoundment fed by a watermill pump. Consequently, it appears that none of the features recorded
during field delineations meet the definition of a WOTUS.

         Waters of the State: Arizona
As described in Section 1.2, Arizona regulates intermittent waters; consequently, the intermittent
features identified in this report may be subject to state regulation.

         Regulated Riparian Areas: Pima and Pinal Counties
As described in Section 1.3, Pima and Pinal counties have some regulations or guidance regarding riparian
areas. The Pima County regulations are more robust and descriptive. The Project ESA intersects 18
riparian washes mapped by Pima County. However, the county regulations require field verification of
these, and other dry washes, that may be crossed by a project. WESTECH documented 33 washes and
canyons, including the San Pedro River, in Pima County that may be subject to county regulation.
The Pinal County mapping is not in a format that can be intersected by the Project ESA in GIS. However,
numerous areas mapped as riparian habitat in Pinal County are intersected by the Project ESA. WESTECH
documented 224 washes in Pinal County that may be subject to county guidance.
